papers.title: Primate Gaze Behavior Reflects Change of Mind in a Naturalistic Navigation Task
papers.abstract: Revising a decision while acting on it is a fundamental aspect of natural behavior, yet the underlying computations are difficult to track in real time. To explore how such belief updates unfold, we tested whether eye movements reveal a subject's change of mind during a naturalistic navigation task with a binary target choice. Humans and monkeys were required to navigate to one of two goal locations presented either simultaneously or sequentially in a virtual environment where explicit position cues were absent. Our findings reveal that gaze continuously tracks the latent variable, including changes of mind. We found that the target tracking accuracy before the second target is even presented during sequential target trials predicts whether the subject's navigational goal persists (first target choice) or changes (second target choice). These results underscore the importance of gaze in action planning and changes of mind, supporting the hypothesis that eye movements embody not only the current latent variable but also its uncertainty.

papers.title: Hemispheric Complementarity is Associated with Distinct Functional and Structural Brain Profiles
papers.abstract: Hemispheric specialization is thought to follow a principle of complementarity, with homotopic functions such as language and attention lateralizing to opposite hemispheres, yet its consistency across individuals and relevance for cognition remain unclear. Using multimodal neuroimaging and twin-family data from 987 Human Connectome Project participants, we identified three sustained attentional lateralization phenotypes (right, left, bilateral) that were independent of handedness, differed by sex, and tracked broad shifts in brain organization, with bilateral individuals showing stronger intrahemispheric and homotopic connectivity. Examining attention and language revealed three multidomain profiles (crowded, mixed, split) reflecting whether functions colocalize within or are distributed across hemispheres. Mixed organization was linked to higher planum polare myelination, whereas crowded organization showed higher fiber density connectivity across dorsal attention-default network. Both phenotypes were heritable, yet neither predicted cognitive performance. These findings reveal a brain organization in which specialization emerges from flexible, heritable patterns linking function, structural connectivity, and myeloarchitecture.

papers.title: Neural Dissociation of Cognitive Maps and Graphs in the Human Brain
papers.abstract: Cognitive maps and graphs offer two distinct ways of organizing knowledge: maps arrange items within a spatial layout, whereas graphs thread them together through experiential transitions. However, spatial proximity and experiential contiguity are typically correlated, and content represented in one format can often be transformed into the other, making their neural representations difficult to disentangle. Here, we orthogonally manipulated Euclidean distance, indexing spatial proximity, and shortest-path distance, indexing experiential contiguity, within the same learned environment. Using fMRI and whole-brain searchlight representational similarity analysis, we identified dissociable representations of these two formats in the human brain. Euclidean distance was represented in the intraparietal sulcus, whereas shortest-path distance was represented in the hippocampal/parahippocampal region and in cortical areas that overlapped substantially with scene-selective regions. ROI analyses further supported the specificity of these representations across regions. Together, these findings provide neural evidence for a dissociation between cognitive maps and cognitive graphs.

papers.title: The anterior insular cortex mediates higher-order threat learning and memory
papers.abstract: Learning about potential threats is indispensable for survival, and its deficits underlie numerous neuropsychiatric disorders. Human brain imaging suggests the anterior insular cortex (AIC) as a key neural correlate of threat learning, yet its mechanistic role remains unclear. They are specifically required when a predictor is temporally separated from an aversive event or when the predictive information is embedded within a diffuse context. In contrast, the AIC is dispensable for elementary, temporally contiguous threat learning. Surprisingly, while the AIC promotes memory formation, it also constrains the level of fear expression during retrieval in a context-dependent manner. This bidirectional control is mediated by the recruitment of distinct AIC neuronal ensembles. Together, we identify a novel circuit mechanism for bidirectional regulation of higher-order threat learning/memory.

papers.title: An astrocytic AMPAR-dependent parity signal preserves synaptic strength
papers.abstract: Astrocytic processes closely associate with excitatory synapses and express AMPARs, positioning them to sense the same glutamate signals as neurons. Astrocytic glutamate sensing through AMPARs, therefore, acts as a parity signal that verifies transmission and stabilizes active synapses.

papers.title: Domain-specific and domain-general signatures of dyscalculia in computational models of behavior and parietal cortex

topics.name: Cognitive and developmental aspects of mathematical skills

papers.abstract: Developmental dyscalculia is a learning disorder characterized by marked difficulties in numerical cognition, yet its cognitive and neural underpinnings remain debated. Competing accounts attribute dyscalculia either to domain-specific imprecise representations of number or to domain-general deficits in the maintenance and integration of numerical information. Here, we test both accounts in 33 adolescents and young adults with dyscalculia and 33 age- and gender-matched controls (15-23 years) who performed a sequential numerosity comparison task during fMRI. Joint computational modeling of choices and response times allowed us to dissociate perceptual and memory noise from decision variables governing the speed-accuracy tradeoff, while complementary neuroimaging analyses characterized neural number representations and their network embedding. Specifically, we quantified the precision of parietal numerosity tuning with numerical population receptive field (nPRF) modeling and derived individualized functional network maps of the same region using community detection algorithms applied to connectivity patterns. Dyscalculic participants showed greater perceptual and memory noise but also a more cautious response criterion, trading speed for accuracy to compensate for representational imprecision. Neurally, the numerosity model explained less variance in parietal cortex, suggesting less precise numerical representations, and individualized network maps assigned less of this cortex to the dorsal attention network and more to a visual network. Rather than supporting a dichotomy between the two accounts, our findings suggest that dyscalculia reflects both less precise numerical representations in parietal cortex and an altered allocation of this cortex to distributed functional systems.

papers.title: Disrupting the Right Inferior Frontal Gyrus Increases Social Brain Activity During Emotion Recognition
papers.abstract: Neuroimaging studies have identified a specialised social brain network that supports emotion recognition and social cognition. This network performs a range of functions that include facial expression recognition and inferring the mental states of others. Studies of neuropsychological patients report that damage to the right inferior frontal gyrus (IFG), the top-down control area in this network, impairs facial expression recognition. To investigate how transient disruption of the right IFG affects the wider social brain we combined transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS) with functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI). Participants (n=20) were scanned across two sessions while performing a delayed match-to-sample emotion recognition task in which happy or fearful expressions were preceded by a congruent or incongruent word cue. Prior to each scan, thetaburst TMS was delivered over the right IFG or over the vertex control site (session order was balanced across participants). A group whole-brain analysis revealed that TMS to the IFG increased neural activity in multiple regions of the social brain network. These included the bilateral temporal pole, precuneus and medial prefrontal cortex (mPFC). This pattern of results shows that the disruption of top-down control mechanisms localised in the IFG alters the neural processing in remote nodes of the social brain network. Our findings are discussed within the wider context of how we recognise and understand the emotions of other people.

papers.title: Plasticity-induced actin polymerization positions endocytic compartments at the bases of stimulated spines
papers.abstract: The endocytic pathway plays key roles in facilitating and regulating synaptic plasticity, but how its components are organized at spines undergoing plasticity is not fully understood. papers.title: Human single-neuron correlates of somatosensation
papers.abstract: Understanding the neural correlates of consciousness poses a central challenge in neuroscience, with longstanding debate over which cortical areas underlie subjective sensory perception. In the tactile domain, posterior parietal cortex (PPC) and primary somatosensory cortex (S1) are candidate cortical substrates for neural correlates of consciousness due to their crucial roles in somatosensory processing. Yet whether and how these regions contribute to conscious tactile perception remains unclear. Here, to address this issue, we leveraged chronic intracortical recordings to simultaneously monitor large ensembles of single neurons in grasp related cortical areas from three participants with tetraplegia while natural vibrotactile stimuli were delivered to a sensate region of the upper limb. We demonstrate that an orchestration of neural activity emerged across the grasp-related parietal-frontal network at near-threshold perception. Within this distributed network, we then focused on PPC and S1. While S1 responses closely tracked the amplitude of the physical stimulus, PPC activity covaried more strongly with awareness and confidence. This single-neuron evidence reveals PPC and S1 have complementary neural codes with PPC transforming physical stimulation into conscious perception whereas S1 is more sensitive to stimulus amplitude.

papers.title: DAP12-deficient microglia adopt a TREM2-independent antigen-presenting state with a glial-to-neuronal cascade in Nasu-Hakola disease
papers.abstract: Nasu-Hakola disease (NHD), a dementia with about 200 cases worldwide, is caused by loss-of-function mutation of TYROBP, encoding DAP12, or its receptor TREM2. We profiled prefrontal cortex and hippocampus from an NHD donor and control by single-nucleus RNA sequencing and mapped the glial changes in situ by spatial transcriptomics. NHD microglia adopted a CIITA-driven, MHC class II-high antigen-presenting state with complement, iron and glycolytic programs and Fc receptors but not the TREM2-dependent lipid program. Astrocytes became pan-reactive and lost metallothionein expression, oligodendrocytes lost mature cells and cholesterol synthesis, and excitatory neurons lost presynaptic and activity programs, consistently between regions and across a published cohort. DAP12 deficiency left microglia in an antigen-presenting state short of the TREM2-dependent arm, accompanied by a glial-to-neuronal cascade.

papers.title: Gradients of local circuit architecture shape stability and information integration across the cortical hierarchy
papers.abstract: The mammalian neocortex is a complex structure with many interacting regions and cell types. Multiple efforts have recently generated large datasets from multiple cortical regions to determine generalizing principles of cortical organization and activity. One such generalizing principle is the concept of a cortical hierarchy - low-dimensional macroscopic gradients of biological properties across cortical areas and a hierarchy of timescales for information processing. Such gradients in properties along a cortical hierarchy may explain how different cortical regions serve different computational roles (i.e. sensory processing versus working memory). We set out to investigate such principles using biologically realistic simulations. Starting from our previously published model of the mouse primary visual cortex (VISp) with updated connectivity reflecting recent large-scale connectomics and synaptic physiology datasets, we generated multiple versions of the cortical circuit model with increased connectivity as measured along the cortical hierarchy. We then measure the resulting neural activity in response to a simulated single-cell photostimulation paradigm and thalamocortical inputs. We found that overall circuit stability increased across the cortical hierarchy, due to both increases in connection density and increases in the relative proportion of SST cells. The results of this study link cortical cell types to population-level activity, generating insight into the function of local circuits across cortex.

papers.title: Mapping the Trade-Offs That Shape Mammalian Brain Network Architecture
papers.abstract: A brain's wiring must satisfy conflicting pressures, from the outside world (be capable) and from the inside (stay within finite resources). These pressures often have opposing requirements. Prior work studies these trade-offs mostly between 2-3 pressures at a time, and thus cannot say how many pressures shape brain wiring or for which trade-off brains decide. To see all possible trade-offs at once and to uncover the set of most important pressures, we generate 25,000 synthetic brain networks and describe each by 29 network properties. We then place 635 human (ages 6-22) and 224 mammalian (12 taxonomic orders) brain networks in this property space. The space is triangular, and follows three pressures: computational capability, robustness to damage, and metabolic efficiency. No network is optimal at all three, and biological brains cluster in one small niche of this triangle. There, they accept higher metabolic cost to gain both robustness and capability. Development and evolution move brains in the same direction; additionally, human maturation first raises capability, and later optimizes for efficiency. This study underscores the triangular trade-off between metabolic efficiency, computational capacity and robustness, and the narrow region brains occupy in this trade-off triangle, visible only from a multi-property, cross-species perspective.

papers.title: Modulation of the speed of Intrinsic Alpha Frequency (IAF) with tACS modulates variability of illusory speech perception
papers.abstract: Navigating the world requires our brains to constantly process a massive influx of information from the environment. One of the most remarkable yet complex feats the human brain performs daily is speech perception. It is a multifaceted, hierarchical process that relies heavily on the integration of auditory and visual cues, particularly in noisy environments. Neural integration of these streams is hypothesized to depend on temporal mechanisms governed by individual alpha frequency (IAF, 8-12 Hz), which serves as a key neural correlate of the temporal binding window (TBW). While IAF has been linked to multisensory integration, its role in shaping multisensory illusions remains largely unexplored. Here, we tested this directly using transcranial alternating current stimulation (tACS) to modulate occipital activity during multisensory conflict. In a two-day protocol involving 27 healthy participants, resting-state EEG was recorded to determine IAF. On Day 2, participants then performed a multisensory speech task involving congruent (pa/, /ta/, /ka/) and incongruent McGurk stimuli (auditory /pa/, visual /ka/), both at baseline and during tACS applied at IAF and offset frequencies (IAF +/- 2 Hz) over occipital electrodes. While accuracy for congruent syllables remained high across conditions, results revealed that tACS significantly reduced the perception of illusory /ta/ percepts during McGurk trials. Finally, using a phenomenological model based on Kuramoto oscillators, we provided a mechanistic explanation for the percentage of illusory responses observed across participants under the influence of tACS at IAF and offsets. This study highlights the potential for targeted neuromodulatory interventions to influence multisensory processing in clinical or professional settings.

papers.title: FMR1 Perturbations Disrupt Sensory Corticostriatal Circuits and Mitochondrial Energetics in Fragile X Syndrome
papers.abstract: Fragile X syndrome (FXS) features sensory, social, and cognitive dysfunction, but how fragile X messenger ribonucleoprotein 1 (FMR1) deficiency disrupts sensory corticostriatal circuitry and whether distinct FMR1 perturbations converge on shared cellular mechanisms remain incompletely defined. We integrated diffusion magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) in individuals with FXS and Fmr1-knockout (KO) mice with projection-defined calcium recording, bidirectional optogenetic manipulation, primary somatosensory cortex (S1)-targeted expression of three patient-associated FMR1 missense variants, regional transcriptomics, and optical manipulation of mitochondrial energetic state. Individuals with FXS exhibited disrupted sensory corticostriatal structural connectivity, with mouse analyses further localizing abnormalities to S1-striatal pathways. Fmr1 deficiency impaired recruitment of the S1-dorsomedial striatum (DMS) pathway during social interaction, and projection-specific manipulation demonstrated that S1-DMS dysfunction contributes to social and cognitive deficits. Three patient-associated FMR1 variants, I234T, E329G, and R586Q, converged on social behavioral deficits, which were improved by S1-DMS activation. Transcriptomic analyses revealed convergent oxidative phosphorylation (OXPHOS)-related mitochondrial remodeling in S1 and DMS across Fmr1 deficiency and variant models. Systemic treatment with the mitochondria-targeted antioxidant MitoQ attenuated novel-location-recognition, social-interaction, and social-novelty deficits in Fmr1-KO mice. Moreover, mt-EcGAPR-based Mitochondrial OptoEnergetic Activation (Mito-OptoEA) enhanced mitochondrial energetic state in S1 and improved novel-location recognition and sociability in both Fmr1-KO and I234T models. Together, these findings define a sensory corticostriatal circuit-metabolic framework for FXS in which S1-DMS circuit dysfunction and convergent mitochondrial energetic abnormalities contribute to FMR1-related social and cognitive phenotypes.

papers.title: Differential utilization of PACAP and glutamate in parabrachial neurons shapes pain and stress
papers.abstract: The external parabrachial nucleus (elPBN) contributes to diverse behaviors, including pain and stress. Neurons in this region use glutamatergic and neuropeptidergic signaling, with pituitary adenylate cyclase-activating polypeptide (PACAP) expressed in a subset of glutamatergic neurons. Deletion of PACAP in elPBN neurons attenuates behavioral responses to stress, but the contribution of PACAP to pain sensitization and of glutamatergic neurotransmission to pain- and stress-related responses remain poorly understood. Here, we show that constitutive loss of PACAP markedly attenuated nerve injury-induced hypersensitivity across heat, pressure, cold and tactile modalities without altering baseline nociception, while also reducing inflammation-induced spontaneous pain-related behavior. Notably, selective deletion of PACAP within elPBN neurons phenocopied the suppression of injury-induced hypersensitivity, but left inflammation- induced pain-related behavior unaffected. Ex vivo optogenetic-assisted circuit mapping showed that activation of PACAP-expressing elPBN terminals elicited glutamatergic transmission onto central amygdala (CeA) PKC{delta}-expressing neurons. Selective deletion of VGluT2 in elPBN neurons reduced nerve injury-induced hypersensitivity but, unlike PACAP deletion, also reduced inflammation-induced pain-related behavior, while leaving stress-induced hypophagia intact. Together, these findings reveal differential requirements for PACAP and glutamatergic neurotransmission within the elPBN across pain- and stress-related behaviors.

papers.title: Developmental prefrontal myelination shapes inhibitory interneuron function and adult social behavior
papers.abstract: Early-life adversity and abnormal myelination are implicated in psychiatric disorders, but how developmental myelination influences adult social cognition remains unclear. Here, we tested whether disrupting developmental myelination in the medial prefrontal cortex (mPFC) impairs adult social behavior. Using complementary genetic strategies in male mice, we suppressed Myelin Regulatory Factor (Myrf)-dependent myelination locally in the juvenile mPFC or broadly in oligodendrocyte-lineage cells. Both approaches selectively impaired adult social novelty preference while sparing sociability, locomotion, and affective behaviors. Focal prefrontal dysmyelination also reduced social dominance. Spatial transcriptomics revealed coupling between myelin-related genes and parvalbumin (PV) interneuron markers in the healthy mPFC, which was disrupted by developmental hypomyelination. Consistent with this transcriptional alteration, PV interneurons showed reduced high-frequency firing despite preserved intrinsic excitability. In the human prefrontal cortex, MBP-PV expression was correlated in controls but not in individuals with schizophrenia. These findings indicate that developmental prefrontal myelination contributes to PV interneuron maturation and suggest that disrupted oligodendrocyte-interneuron coordination may contribute to impaired social recognition.

papers.title: A neural circuit algorithm for action grammar
papers.abstract: How does the brain generate sequences of discrete elements, such as actions or words, that follow an abstract rule (a grammar)? Motivated by an experiment in which monkeys learned to draw multi-object images according to grammatical rules, we trained a recurrent neural network to generate sequences Am Bn: producing shape A m times, then B n times, or vice versa. Our findings are threefold. First, the network plans the sequence by moving to an initial state encoding m and n along orthogonal directions for upcoming execution. Second, the network repeats each shape by progressing along a shape-specific manifold. Third, transitions from Am to Bn follow parallel trajectories between manifolds across values of n, thus preserving n. Each of these is an experimentally testable prediction. The network generalizes to longer novel sequences by starting further along the same orthogonal directions. These results reveal a neural circuit implementation of a symbolic algorithm for generating rule-based action sequences.

papers.title: Newborns modulate and synchronise their Non-Nutritive Sucking behaviour to the temporal structure of sound
papers.abstract: Sensorimotor synchronization, the ability to align motor behaviour with the temporal structure of external stimuli, is thought to emerge gradually during development, but its origins remain unclear. Here, we investigated whether newborns can adapt their sucking behaviour and synchronise it to the temporal structure of auditory stimuli within the first days of life. Forty-one healthy full-term newborns (24-72 hours old) were exposed to two three-minute auditory streams differing in temporal structure: a highly structured stream with a stable temporal pattern and a highly variant stream with greater temporal variability, while their non-nutritive sucking (NNS) was continuously recorded. We assessed changes in NNS frequency and pressure and quantified NNS-sound coupling using magnitude-squared coherence at frequencies distinctive to each auditory stream. Structured stimulation promoted a more organised NNS, with more suck bursts than the variant stream, and increased sucking vigour, with a transiently higher suck peak rate during the first minute relative to the variant stream and greater suck pressure relative to silence. Coherence analyses revealed that coherence was selectively higher at the frequencies distinctive to each auditory stream, both for the structured and the highly variant stimulus. These findings show that, within hours of birth, NNS behaviour can selectively align with stimulus-specific temporal regularities, even when these are weakly predictable and lack a dominant periodicity. This early capacity to extract temporal structure and coordinate motor behaviour may provide a foundation for the subsequent development of sensorimotor synchronisation.

papers.title: Mapping reward processing circuits: the orbitofrontal-nucleus accumbens white matter pathways and their associations to psychopathological traits
papers.abstract: Dysfunctions in reward circuits, including projections from the orbitofrontal cortex (OFC) to the nucleus accumbens (NAcc), have been implicated in psychopathology. The OFC is functionally divided into the medial OFC (mOFC), which processes rewards, and the lateral OFC (lOFC), which responds to non-reward or punishment stimuli. Diffusion-weighted imaging data from 165 participants (aged 22 - 35, 53% male) in the Human Connectome Project (HCP) were analysed using spherical deconvolution tractography. MegaTrack, a novel tool, enabled tract segmentation via a single manual dissection mapped back to native space. Virtual dissection identified four bilateral pathways connecting the lOFC and mOFC to the NAcc, from which fractional anisotropy (FA) was extracted, and an lOFC/mOFC ratio was computed. Psychopathological traits were measured using HCP Achenbach Adult Self-Report scores. The lOFC-NAcc pathway showed positive associations with psychopathology and the mOFC-NAcc pathway negative associations. The lOFC/mOFC ratio emerged as a stronger predictor than individual pathways, with significant associations for depression, somatic problems, anti-social personality traits, and inattention. Effects were lateralized to the left hemisphere. These findings show that the lOFC-NAcc and mOFC-NAcc pathways can be structurally separated with tractography and display opposing correlations with psychopathological traits in a healthy population. Their ratio may index reward-processing dysfunction, and future research should test whether it is sensitive to dysfunction in clinical populations.

We measured performance in an odd-one-out color constancy task, with objects rendered in complex lighting environments. Observers identified the odd object among four objects, with two rendered under each of two lighting environments, sampled from a wide range of object orientations and camera positions. Constancy was high. The presence of a surrounding context increased accuracy. Gloss provided no measurable benefit. We also tested a condition in which the global color impression provided misleading information about the lighting environment, but this impaired performance only slightly. These findings suggest that human color constancy remains robust even under complex lighting environments, contrary to predictions of many simple models of illuminant discounting.

papers.title: Continuous amyloid staging complements global amyloid burden in early Alzheimer's disease
authors: For the Alzheimers Disease Neuroimaging Initiative,
papers.abstract: Introduction: Early Alzheimer's disease (AD) staging remains challenging because clinical categories and global amyloid PET measures provide only coarse characterization of disease progression. We developed a continuous amyloid staging score from regional amyloid PET to complement global amyloid burden. Methods: Using longitudinal florbetapir PET from the Alzheimer's Disease Neuroimaging Initiative (ADNI), we trained an end-to-end deep learning model to directly estimate a continuous amyloid staging score. We evaluated longitudinal consistency, its relationship with global amyloid burden, regional contributors to early-stage variation, and whether the staging score stratified subsequent memory decline among participants matched for baseline global amyloid burden. Cognitive analyses were replicated in A4+LEARN. Results: The staging score better preserved longitudinal visit order than existing amyloid staging approaches. During early disease stages, it captured regional amyloid variation despite relatively stable global amyloid burden. Among participants with similar baseline global amyloid burden, higher staging scores were associated with faster subsequent memory decline in both ADNI and A4+LEARN. Discussion: A continuous amyloid staging score complements global amyloid burden for early AD staging and cognitive risk stratification. Keywords: Alzheimer's disease; amyloid PET; disease staging; cognitive decline

papers.title: Linear NeuroPaint: An Efficient Baseline for Cross-Session Neural Alignment and Inpainting
papers.abstract: Large-scale Neuropixels recordings sample many brain areas, but no single experimental session records every area of interest. NeuroPaint, a transformer-based autoencoder, integrates such recordings by aligning area-specific latent dynamics across sessions and "inpainting" activity in unrecorded areas. Could a linear model, which would be computationally efficient and potentially more interpretable, suffice to achieve this? To address this question, we introduce Linear NeuroPaint, a linear variant of NeuroPaint, and evaluate it on two multi-area Neuropixels datasets. Linear NeuroPaint achieves strong predictive performance on recorded areas, however, it is less accurate than nonlinear models at cross-area inpainting, despite extensive hyperparameter optimization. Moreover, its parameters are not readily interpretable: incomplete cross-session alignment leads parameter-defined neuron clusters to exhibit heterogeneous response profiles. Together, these results show that linear transformations are insufficient for cross-session alignment and cross-area prediction. Nevertheless, Linear NeuroPaint provides a computationally efficient baseline for benchmarking multi-session neural models.

papers.title: A Bayesian approach to volumetric analysis in rare neurodegenerative disorders
papers.abstract: Identifying regional brain atrophy is critical for understanding neurodegenerative disorders. Traditionally, group comparisons rely on frequentist statistics, utilising $p$-values and point estimates that offer limited characterization of uncertainty. Bayesian methods provide an alternative by estimating effect sizes and credible intervals while incorporating prior knowledge and uncertainty. This study evaluated the feasibility of Bayesian hierarchical modelling to assess regional brain atrophy in Progressive Supranuclear Palsy (PSP) and Corticobasal Syndrome (CBS) compared to healthy controls. Participants meeting diagnostic criteria for CBS or PSP, together with healthy controls, were recruited from the Cambridge Centre for Parkinson-plus. Grey matter volume, cortical thickness, and subcortical volumes were derived using FreeSurfer for 210 cortical and 36 subcortical regions defined by the Human Brainnetome Atlas. Participants with PSP were classified into Richardson syndrome (PSP-RS), corticobasal syndrome variant (PSP-CBS), frontal variant (PSP-F), and other presentations (PSP-Other). Bayesian hierarchical ANOVA models with appropriate priors were used to estimate group differences. Regions of practical equivalence (ROPE) were calculated to assess evidence of meaningful group effects. A total of 428 people were included (113 PSP-RS, 30 PSP-CBS, 23 PSP-Other, 19 PSP-F, 81 CBS, and 162 healthy controls). For grey matter volume, there was evidence of whole brain volume loss compared to controls for all disease groups except PSP-Other, which showed evidence of no difference. For cortical thickness, there was evidence of global cortical thinning in CBS compared to controls, but for no other group. For subcortical volume all groups showed evidence of volume loss compared to controls. Patterns of regional atrophy were identified in keeping with previous literature, with the largest effect observed in the left pre-motor thalamus (30\% reduction in CBS). There was greater loss of subcortical volume in PSP-RS compared to other PSP subgroups. Bayesian hierarchical modelling provides a feasible framework for quantifying regional brain atrophy, with interpretable effect size estimates and uncertainty measures. This approach complements conventional statistical methods, particularly in the assessment of rare neurodegenerative and neuropsychiatric disorders.

papers.title: A Computational Model Captures Orexin-Dependent Modulation of Memory Consolidation.
papers.abstract: Hippocampal sharp-wave ripple (SWR) events occur during post-experience rest and sleep and play a significant role in memory consolidation. Recent ex vivo studies have found orexin-driven neuromodulatory effects on SWR parameters and proposed that they can influence memory consolidation. Additionally, behavioral studies demonstrate contradictory results regarding orexinergic effects on memory acquisition depending on task structure and intervention time. This inconsistency, along with the diffuse spread of orexin receptors (OXR) in the CA1 and CA3 hippocampus, challenges theoretical interpretation of orexinergic effects on memory. To reconcile this problem, we propose a rate-based model linking orexinergic tone-dependent SWR statistics to memory performance. The model combines an encoding module whose gain scales with the global orexinergic tone with a consolidation module driven by OX2R-specific replay dynamics. The model is based on a plasticity rule that considers SWR events as the unit of induction. Therefore, weight change requires sufficient replay content and depolarizing drive. We observed that, depending on the task structure, encoding-dominant learning benefits discrimination as the orexin drive increases. Consolidation-dominant learning shows a non-monotonic relationship with an internal optimum level of orexinergic tone. This interaction highlights that stronger truncation at higher receptor engagement shortens memory replay and reduces the efficacy of the consolidation process. The model predicts that the optimal regime depends on task complexity reflected in sequence length. Together, these results demonstrate how task demands determine whether increased orexinergic drive enhances or impairs effective consolidation and SWR-dependent replay in the hippocampus.

papers.title: Identifying Network Factors Driving Changes in Brain Connectivity During Aging via Stochastic Actor-Oriented Models
authors: for the Alzheimer's Disease Neuroimaging Initiative,
papers.abstract: Brain network organization emerges from ongoing network dynamics that continuously create, maintain, and reorganize connectivity patterns. At both the structural and functional levels, these dynamics shape network evolution throughout the lifespan. Here, we introduce a data-driven framework based on Stochastic Actor-Oriented Models (SAOMs), which model longitudinal network changes as a process of local edge formation and dissolution driven by local-connectivity factors. Applied to functional and structural brain networks from an aging cohort, the resulting models recovered a set of interacting mechanisms that collectively promote hub formation, short-range connectivity, and modular organization. These factors were derived through a novel data-driven factor-selection procedure rather than specified a priori, allowing network mechanisms underlying longitudinal change to be identified directly from observations. Functional networks exhibited substantially higher rates of change than structural networks, suggesting more frequent opportunities for network maintenance and reorganization. Structural networks additionally showed despecification in the hub-forming mechanisms with cognitive impairment. These results support a view of brain network organization as an actively maintained process emerging from ongoing local connectivity dynamics. More broadly, this framework provides a general approach for studying longitudinal network dynamics through the estimation of network-generating mechanisms over time.

papers.title: Encephalitic alphavirus infection reduces neurite outgrowth and downregulates Rho GTPase pathways in human iPSC-derived neurospheres
papers.abstract: Venezuelan equine encephalitis virus (VEEV) is a re-emerging neurotropic arbovirus, which affects the developing human brain, potentially leading to miscarriage, stillbirth, or long-term neurological sequelae. Currently, the mechanisms underlying these sequelae remain largely elusive. Using human induced pluripotent stem cell (iPSC)-derived neurospheres as a model for brain development, we show that both human neurons and glial cells are susceptible to VEEV infection. Microscopy-based quantification reveals that VEEV impairs neurite outgrowth in the human neurospheres. To mechanistically assess these observations, we performed multi-omics analyses of VEEV-infected neurospheres and demonstrate translational shutoff including downregulation of Rho GTPase pathways. The transcriptional and proteome profile is indicative of reduced actin cytoskeleton dynamics and consequently migratory defects of cells in the neurospheres. Shotgun secretomics moreover revealed downmodulation of neurite outgrowth associated proteins including midkine (MDK), amyloid-beta precursor protein (APP) and microtubule-associated protein 1B (MAP1B). Our findings reveal mechanistic insights into how VEEV infection impairs neuronal development and demonstrate that neurospheres are a powerful platform for assessing teratogenic effects of viruses on brain development.

papers.title: Neuronal sex identity shapes social buffering of defensive freezing behaviour in fruit flies
papers.abstract: Sex differences are pervasive across the animal kingdom1,2, shaped by reproductive strategies, ecological roles, and physiological demands. Neurobiological studies have largely focused on sex differences in reproduction and aggression3,4, leaving understudied how sex shapes other survival-relevant behaviours such as responses to predatory threats. Previous work in vertebrates uncovered sex differences in individual defence responses deployed by rats5 and in social modulation of freezing responses in zebrafish6. The origin of these differences and their potential underlying neuronal circuitry remain however unknown. Here we characterise defensive responses to a visual threat of female and male fruit flies tested alone and in groups. Individually, defensive responses are comparable across sex, with similar freezing levels and moderately increased escape responses in males. In groups, however, we uncovered strong sex differences in freezing as males show consistently shorter freezing bouts, reflecting a stronger social buffering effect than in females. Using a generalised linear mixed model, we demonstrate that the shorter freezes of male flies, when tested in groups, are not explained by well-known locomotor differences between sexes7,8. Although males move more and faster, generating stronger social motion cues that mediate the "safety in numbers" effect in female flies9,10, their response to the surrounding motion is not increased. We further identify the nervous system as the source of this sex-dimorphic behaviour by feminising males through pan-neuronal ectopic expression of transformer, a key regulator of the cell-autonomous sex-differentiation pathway. Finally, we ruled out the visual projection neurons, lobula columnar neurons 11 (LC11), detectors of social motion10, as the source of the neuronal-sex differences observed. This study identifies a neuronal origin of sex differences in socially modulated behaviour that extends beyond sex-specific behavioural modules or locomotor function, important to understand differential impact on survival upon threat across sexes.

papers.title: Neuron types and distribution of a Drosophila driver line collection
papers.abstract: Cell type designations label uniquely-identifiable groups of related cells that typically function in similar ways. papers.title: Learning Interpretable Switching Dynamics in Shared Neural-Behavioral Latent Space
papers.abstract: Modern recording technologies enable simultaneous measurement of high-dimensional neural activity and rich behavioral variables, creating both an opportunity and a modeling challenge: identifying the shared latent structure that mediates the brain-behavior relationship and the underlying dynamics through which it evolves across behavioral states. Existing approaches focus on different parts of this challenge: shared representation learning methods identify neural-behavioral subspaces but typically do not model dynamical structure, while dynamical models capture temporal variation and discrete state transitions in neural activity, but do not explicitly disentangle shared neural-behavioral structure from modality-specific variability. We introduce Switching Shared Latent Dynamics (SSLD), a unified framework that learns a latent representation shared between neural activity and behavior and endows this shared space with nonlinear switching recurrent dynamics to reflect the hypothesis that behaviorally relevant neural representations exhibit structured dynamical changes across behavioral states. Complementary private latent variables capture modality-specific variability, providing a window into neural activity that does not directly interact with behavior. We evaluate SSLD on a simulated dataset and four diverse experimental datasets spanning species, brain regions, and recording modalities: monkey motor and premotor cortex during reaching, somatosensory cortex during a bump task, widefield calcium imaging across mouse dorsal cortex during (a) self-initiated decision-making and (b) spontaneous movements. Across all four datasets, SSLD accurately reconstructs neural and behavioral signals, recovers discrete states in the dynamics that align with experimentally defined behavioral epochs, and isolates behaviorally-relevant neural information in the shared latent while preserving private neural variability. Ablations confirm that shared representation learning, behavioral supervision, and switching dynamics each contribute to performance. SSLD offers an interpretable approach to modeling shared neural-behavioral dynamics that complements ongoing efforts toward foundation models for neuroscience.

papers.title: A network model of path control
papers.abstract: We present a network model that enables a navigating agent to shape the spatial and temporal structure of its paths through its environment. The model is inspired by the insect fan-shaped body. In it, a recurrent neural network receives an input that encodes an agent's velocity vector. Meanwhile, network activity determines the setpoint of a control loop that influences this velocity vector through motor outputs. The network thus guides future movement using memory of past movement. We illustrate how the network's dynamics determine the trajectory features it extracts to produce the setpoint. We then relate the joint dynamics of network activity and the agent's velocity vector to the structure of the resulting paths. This network can produce paths suitable for different forms of exploration. It can also stabilize movements initiated by lower-level systems. Our analyses illustrate how recurrent neural dynamics and memory can shape behavior when embedded in closed loops.

papers.title: Lateral recurrence dynamically refines visual representations for task performance
papers.abstract: Recurrent connections are pervasive in visual cortex, and visual representations evolve as recurrent processing unfolds. Yet the mechanism underlying this temporal transformation remains poorly understood. To address this question, we trained recurrent convolutional networks on face and object recognition and tested them on a parametric stimulus set in which category, identity, and pose were systematically varied. This design isolates how lateral recurrence reshapes neural-population representational geometry and single-unit tuning across recurrent timesteps. Within the trained domain, recurrence increased the separability between identities in deeper layers, while leaving the non-trained domain representations largely unchanged. Gating lateral weights abolished the across-timestep gain in trained-domain identity decoding, demonstrating that lateral recurrence drives this refinement. At the single-unit level, recurrence strengthened the correlation between each unit's category preference and its within-domain identity sensitivity, providing a unit-level mechanism for the population-level changes. These results identify lateral recurrence as a dynamic mechanism for refining learned representational structure within a fixed neural population, yielding testable predictions for time-resolved recordings in domain-selective cortex.

papers.title: Pharmacokinetic properties of Ogerin and its regulation of post-ischemia signaling in mice
papers.abstract: Ogerin, a positive regulator of GPR68, reduces infarct volume and attenuates blood-brain barrier (BBB) leakage post transient middle cerebral artery occlusion (tMCAO). These data support the potential use of Ogerin for ischemic protection. For therapeutic interventions, tissue distribution, kinetics, and brain penetration are important characteristics for a compound. For these reasons, we performed liquid chromatography-mass spectrometry (LC-MS) analysis of Ogerin in mice. At 3 hours following intraperitoneal (IP) injection, liver exhibited highest level of Ogerin among all major organs assessed. We further analyzed time-dependent changes in Ogerin concentration in serum following intravenous delivery. Brain Ogerin level was ~140 ng/g at 2 hour and ~0.06ng/g at 24 hours. The brain-to-serum ratio of Ogerin was ~0.6 at 5 hr. To determine the effect of Ogerin on signaling, we collected samples 24 hours after tMCAO with or without Ogerin delivered and performed Western blotting. Consistent with the diminished level of Ogerin in brain at 24 hour, tMCAO increased similar changes in phosphorylation of PKA substrates and PKC substrates in vehicle- and Ogerin-treated groups. The pharmacokinetic data suggests that Ogerin is effective mainly during acute hours after injection. This finding generates important insights on the design of effective protocol for Ogerin delivery to potentiate GPR68 function in vivo.

papers.title: Bone regulates locomotion by sustaining motoneuronal mitochondrial function
papers.abstract: Body-brain communication is crucial for optimal neuronal performance across the lifespan, yet whether peripheral organs regulate spinal cord motoneuron (MN) function through circulating molecules remains unknown. The expression of hormone receptors by spinal MNs raises the possibility that circulating cues allow the spinal cord to sense the body's energetic state and sustain motor activity. Here, we show that the bone-derived hormones osteocalcin (OCN) signals on spinal MNs via its receptor GPR158. GPR158 is selectively enriched in spinal cholinergic MNs, and its loss, globally or specifically in spinal MNs, or the one of OCN, impairs locomotor function and reduces choline acetyltransferase (ChAT) levels. Mechanistically, OCN signaling through GPR158 fine-tunes autophagy, mitophagy and mitochondrial activity in spinal MNs. Restoring any of these processes, by pharmacologically inducing mitophagy or chemogenetically activating mitochondria, is sufficient to rescue the locomotor deficits of Gpr158-deficient mice. Finally, OCN restoration in aged mice reverses age-related locomotor decline through a mechanism that requires MN autophagy and mitophagy. This study reveals that through OCN, the skeleton influences motor functions by fine-tuning motoneuronal mitochondria, and suggests that age-related motor decline is, at least in part, reversible.

papers.title: Expert and Novice Visuomotor Strategies in a Sequential Football Task Reflect Distinct Generative Models
papers.abstract: In visuomotor sequential tasks, chaining actions smoothly requires tight coordination between sensory and motor systems to deal with competing demands, such as reducing uncertainty about future opportunities for action while controlling ongoing ones. In a football-based decision-making task, experts and novices used different strategies to overcome these competing demands, demonstrating a proactive and a sequential visuomotor strategy, respectively. We propose a computational explanation of expertise-related difference in policy selection, grounded in the active inference framework. We simulated the selection of sequence of actions using a partially observable Markov decision process (POMDP) model, and we manipulated three parameters: the reward structure, the prior beliefs about state transition, and the sensory precision. Simulations showed that selection of the proactive strategy relied on strong prior beliefs, high sensory precision and high valuation of fast passing. Conversely, the sequential policy was selected when rapid performance was not highly valued, or under noisy prior beliefs, or lower level of sensory precision. Decreasing sensory precision and adding noise in prior beliefs also decreased decision accuracy. These results suggest that policy selection leading to novice or expert visuomotor strategy reflects differences in the underlying generative model, particularly in how agents value different aspects of the task.

papers.title: Retinotopic organization of head-orienting vectors in the pigeon ventral lateral geniculate nucleus
papers.abstract: The ventral lateral geniculate nucleus (GLv) is a conserved retinorecipient structure positioned between visual and premotor systems, yet its role in visuomotor transformations remains poorly understood. Here, we examined whether the pigeon GLv contains a spatially organized motor representation linking visual-field locations to orienting movements. Anatomical tracing identified descending projections from neurons in the GLv inner lamina (GLv-li) through pretectal and tegmental regions toward pontine targets. GLv-li projection neurons are GABAergic, yet electrical microstimulation of GLv-li in awake pigeons evoked rapid head movements followed by smaller eye movements. Each stimulation locus produced a reproducible characteristic motor vector whose direction and duration were largely insensitive to stimulation parameters, whereas movement amplitude and velocity approached site-specific plateaus. Movements initiated from different head positions were better explained by repetition of a fixed displacement than by convergence toward a common spatial goal. Critically, motor-vector direction was systematically related to the direction of the visual receptive field represented at the same GLv locus, while motor-vector amplitude covaried with receptive-field eccentricity. These defining features persisted after optic tectum ablation. papers.title: Dispelling the Plateau Assumption: Case-Based Evidence for Language Recovery in Chronic-Post Stroke Aphasia
papers.abstract:
ObjectiveRecovery from post-stroke aphasia is traditionally thought to plateau within a year after stroke. As such, no studies have characterized long-term recovery using comprehensive behavioral assessment and longitudinal functional MRI. We sought to characterize behavioral and neuroplastic changes over nearly six years in a patient with chronic post-stroke aphasia.

MethodsA patient with chronic left hemisphere stroke underwent behavioral assessment and task-based fMRI at 9, 22, 33 and 71 months after stroke. Testing assessed auditory comprehension, semantic and phonological processing, naming, reading, spelling, motor speech, and executive function. Task-related activation during an adaptive semantic matching paradigm was quantified within language and semantic regions of interest.

ResultsBehavior improved across multiple language domains. WAB-R Aphasia Quotient increased from 49.2 to 69.2, along with the large gains in word finding, connected speech, reading and spelling, whereas auditory comprehension remained relatively stable. fMRI demonstrated progressively increasing activation within left-hemisphere language regions, reaching normative range by the final assessment, along with increasing activation in semantic/executive regions.

DiscussionRecovery of language production abilities can continue for years after stroke, supported by neuroplastic changes in the brain. Neurologists should inform stroke survivors that aphasia recovery can continue indefinitely after stroke.

papers.title: Information regimes in population-graph neuroimaging: cohort context and implementation-dependent evaluation sensitivity
papers.abstract: Population-graph models aggregate a query subject with an unlabeled cohort, so their reported performance can depend on the evaluation regime rather than on predictive information alone. Evaluation context has two separable axes: the visibility of the cohort during training, and the context available at inference. We study the training-time axis under a protocol fixed before analysis, on an ABIDE-I cohort of 871 subjects (20 acquisition sites). Two population-graph implementations are compared: a learned/adaptive graph (EV-GCN) and a static weighted graph (Parisot-GCN). Within each implementation the cohort, connectivity features, outer splits and training and selection rules are held fixed, and only the information available to the graph varies. The primary estimand is the implementation-by-training-context interaction: the difference between the P0-to-P1 AUC changes of the two implementations ({Delta}{Delta}AUC). Across three preselected outer splits (666, 1024, 2024) the direction is consistent and positive, with observed interaction range 0.06285-0.13090; uncertainty is assessed separately within each split by paired subject and site-cluster bootstrap resampling and is reported per split. Splits are replication units: they are not pooled and no cross-split average is reported, so the result is not a claim of invariance to arbitrary splits. These findings tie reported population-graph performance to the evaluation information regime and motivate explicit reporting of cohort visibility. The contribution is methodological: a two-axis taxonomy of information regimes, preselected cross-split evidence that the sensitivity of reported performance to cohort context depends on the implementation, and a reusable reporting checklist.

papers.title: Motivational incentives improve working memory performance by enhancing memory-based representations rather than altering response strategies
papers.abstract: Motivational incentives are known to improve working memory (WM) when items differ in value, but whether they enhance performance when all items are equally valued, and if so, by what mechanism, remains unclear. Improvements could reflect enhanced memory-based representations or speed-accuracy trade-offs, whereby incentives promote slower, more cautious responding without improving memory itself. Here, we tested these alternatives across two experiments using an auditory WM task in which incentives varied across trials, but all items on a trial were equally incentivised. In Experiment 1,we allowed participants to resubmit their responses if desired. Reward-related improvements in WM performance were selectively observed when memory load was high, and only at serial positions associated with greater interference. These improvements were also dissociated from systematic response slowing and resubmission behaviour. This indicated that the benefits of incentives were unlikely to be attributable to response caution. Critically, in Experiment 2, motivational benefits persisted under strict response deadlines, where speed cannot be traded for accuracy. Computational modelling showed that reward selectively improved the precision of memory-based responses without reducing guessing. Together, these findings indicate that motivational incentives improve WM by enhancing the quality of memory-based representations, rather than by strategic slowing or altering response strategies.

papers.title: Thalamocortical credit routing from the basal ganglia and cerebellum: anatomical constraints and circuit principles
papers.abstract: Animals learn to select actions that maximize reward in complex environments. A central challenge in this process is credit routing: behavioral outcomes must be routed back to the neural populations that contributed to generating the relevant actions. One possible route is through thalamocortical pathways conveying learning signals from the basal ganglia and cerebellum, where plasticity is shaped by reward-prediction errors. However, how these pathways route such signals back to specific cortical circuits remains unclear. To address this question, we combined anatomical circuit mapping in mice with closed-loop circuit modeling. Anterograde transsynaptic tracing revealed that thalamic neurons receiving input from the substantia nigra pars reticulata or the lateral cerebellar nucleus were largely segregated, with partial overlap in the ventromedial thalamus. Nevertheless, their cortical axons shared a pronounced enrichment in layer 1a, most prominently in secondary motor cortex. In a brain- wide synergistic loop-circuit model, learning was enhanced when both pathways delivered additive and gain-modulating feedback aligned with the cortical action readout. Local activity- based calibration established this alignment, whereas dendritic-spike- and reward-prediction- error-dependent thalamocortical plasticity further refined behavioral output. Module-specific feedback was essential for a brain-machine interface task requiring the simultaneous conditioning of multiple target neurons. Together, these findings define a credit-routing architecture in which laminar convergence, plastic alignment, and modular feedback link parallel subcortical learning systems to cortical action representations.

papers.title: Neural circuit mechanisms for multi-tasking
papers.abstract: Neural activity during performance of a cognitive or motor task is often described as lying on a low-dimensional manifold in the space of all possible activity patterns. When multiple tasks are performed, an individual brain region's activity may generate multiple such manifolds. Several models have been introduced to explain this capability, each with different assumptions concerning architecture and inputs. Here, we develop a theory of multi-tasking according to which models and experimental paradigms can be organized. We introduce a distinction between sequential and simultaneous multi-tasking, the performance of one task at a time or multiple in parallel. We show that interference between tasks often prevents multi-tasking and introduce a model of ``task barcodes" that circumvents this problem and parameterizes a neuronal population's task selectivity. Our theory reveals categorical distinctions between neural circuit mechanisms supporting multi-tasking that can be probed using physiological recordings.

papers.title: Psychedelics restructure information in the human brain
papers.abstract: How do psychedelic drugs alter human brain function? Answering this question relies on our ability to understand how information is stored, transferred, and transformed across the cortex. Here, we leverage a precise mathematical framework for multivariate information decomposition to construct the first comprehensive picture of these processes across five compounds: LSD, psilocybin, ketamine, DMT and 5-MeO-DMT (N=80). We provide a formal and empirical explanation of major prior results, revealing sets of competing underlying phenomena masked by extant approaches. We extend this analysis to novel higher-order phenomena, and we demonstrate how all of these observations can emerge from a minimal generative model in which neural populations operate with reduced self-coupling. In sum, our results suggest that the psychedelic brain is one in which cortical populations become alike, but not necessarily together. This has important implications for models of how psychedelics reorganize brain dynamics to alter subjective experience and alleviate mental health conditions.

papers.title: Glia-enriched human brain organoids for studying developmental alterations in leukodystrophies
papers.abstract: Leukodystrophies (LKD) comprise mostly inherited white matter disorders whose developmental origins and underlying pathomechanisms remain poorly understood. Progress has been limited by restricted access to human primary tissue and by the inability of animal models to fully recapitulate human neurodevelopment. Human induced pluripotent stem cell-derived neural organoids provide an alternative approach, but most culture systems do not capture later, glia-rich developmental stages relevant to these diseases. Recent studies have shown that appropriate patterning cues and long in vitro differentiation can generate neuroglial spheroids comprising multiple neuronal and macroglial populations, including mature oligodendrocytes. Here, we adapt the human oligodendrocyte (hOLS) spheroid platform to establish 3D models of globoid cell leukodystrophy (GLD), 4H leukodystrophy (4H), and Canavan disease (CD). Here we adapt this organoid platform to establish 3D models of globoid cell leukodystrophy (GLD), 4H leukodystrophy (4H), and Canavan disease (CD). Across 150 days of differentiation, hOLS from different genetic backgrounds displayed largely comparable growth kinetics and developmental trajectories, comprising multiple neuroglial cell types with predominantly ventral forebrain and midbrain identities. Comparison of LKD and control hOLS revealed both shared and disease-specific alterations, with prominent transcriptional changes in lysosomal, metabolic, and stress-response pathways. Lineage-resolved pathway analysis further identified signatures across individual LKDs, including mitochondrial and translational stress in GLD glial lineages, disruption of RNA metabolic and cell-cycle pathways in 4H, and prominent astrocyte-centered metabolic dysregulation in CD. Our results establish hOLS as a human 3D in vitro platform for studying the impact of LKD-associated genetic variants on early neural development and for dissecting lineage-specific disease vulnerability.

papers.title: Design and Test Novel EEG Electrode Attachments for Type 4 Afro-textured Hairstyles
papers.abstract: Black participants remain underrepresented in electroencephalography (EEG) research, partly because current EEG devices work poorly with dense, coily Type 4 Afro-textured hair. Research-grade EEG typically wires electrodes on a cap, and therefore the electrodes often fail to reach the scalp through dense, Afro-textured hair. Protocols that ask Black participants to unbraid or restyle protective hairstyles add burdens that discourage enrollment in research studies. To address this, we designed and tested 3D-printed attachments that fit onto an EEG electrode and anchored it directly in the hair, using the hairstyle itself as the mounting structure. We fabricated three design configurations for natural Afro-textured hair, cornrows/braids, and twists/microlocs. Seventeen healthy adults with Type 4a-4c hair used electrode attachments that matched their hairstyle. During a single visit, EEG was recorded with 16 conventional cap electrodes defined by the international 10-20 system and with 16 electrodes using novel electrode attachments anchored directly to their hair. Participants completed resting and walking trials with each system. Electrode-to-scalp distance and gel volume were measured during setup. Electrode disconnection, impedance, signal quality (i.e. peak alpha power and aperiodic (1/f) component), and comfort level were measured throughout the data collection. Compared with the conventional cap, the novel attachments reduced electrode-to-scalp distance, gel use, and impedance. Twenty percent of the conventional cap electrodes failed to connect to the scalp compared with 0.1% of novel electrodes. Impedance rose across trials for the conventional cap, whereas the novel attachments showed a smaller increase and maintained lower impedance throughout. Signal quality was significantly better using the novel attachments, while comfort level did not differ between systems. In conclusion, hair-anchored electrode attachment may present a feasible alternative to conventional cap-based EEG for people with Type 4 hair, yielding more usable channels and better signal quality, and supporting more inclusive EEG acquisition.

papers.title: Transient Vascular Cell Integration and Intrinsic Media-Stimulated Endothelial Activation Reveal Diabetic Retinopathy Signatures in Human Retinal Organoids
papers.abstract: Retinal organoids (ROs) model human retinogenesis but remain avascular and lack immune components, limiting their utility for studying vascular retinopathies. We generated vascular organoids (VOrs) from human pluripotent stem cells and evaluated their integration into developing ROs. Dissociated VOr cells (day 12 or day 30) were seeded onto 2D retinal neuroepithelium before 3D transition, followed by long-term culture to day 210. VOr derived cells migrated into ROs and transiently persisted. V30 ROs preserved retinal lamination, major neuronal subtypes and light evoked retinal ganglion cell responses comparable to non vascularised controls, whereas media-only ROs cultured in proangiogenic conditions showed structural disorganisation and reduced neuronal survival. Single-cell RNA sequencing revealed an endogenous, inflammatory endothelial-like population with partial endothelial-to-mesenchymal features and a perivascular fibroblast-like cluster in pro-angiogenic media only RO controls. The endothelial-like cell cluster was significantly enriched for genes upregulated in human retinal endothelial cells exposed to high glucose, indicating a diabetic retinopathy like transcriptional state. Microglia like and border associated macrophage populations were present across all conditions, with developmental shifts in morphology and marker expression. Our findings define conditions under which vascular cells can be incorporated into human ROs without disrupting retinal architecture, while uncovering an intrinsic capacity for inflammatory endothelial activation that partially recapitulates diabetic retinopathy. This work advances the engineering of vascularised, immunocompetent retinal models and highlights endogenous vascular immune programmes that must be considered when modelling retinal disease in vitro.

papers.title: cyto7: an open, vertex-level cortical type atlas of the human cortex
papers.abstract: The cerebral cortex is organized along a gradient of laminar complexity, indexed principally by the emergence and granularity of layer IV and by the size of layer III neuron somata, and cortical types are the ordered categories along it. The Structural Model builds on that gradient to predict laminar connectivity, plasticity and disease vulnerability (Barbas and Rempel-Clower, 1997; Garcia-Cabezas et al., 2019). Existing digital cortical-type maps are area-level: they assign one type per classical area and cannot represent a type boundary that runs through an area. We release cyto7, an open, vertex-level, seven-type cortical-type atlas delineated on the fsaverage surface following the Garcia-Cabezas protocol and revised by the protocol's authors. We distribute the atlas with a reusable quality-control and support framework. A topological audit reports the map against four spatial rules that follow from cortical type analysis and the dual origin of the neocortex theory: neighbouring vertices differ by at most one type, the least complex cortex forms one continuous limbic belt, eulaminate II forms a single matrix enclosing a few holes, and eulaminate III and koniocortex form isolated islands. These were imposed during construction rather than tested, and the audit reports what imposing them cost. A vertex-wise benchmark against the existing area-level map, one type per von Economo-Koskinas area, shows exact agreement at 52.5% of vertices, with disagreement almost always a single level and concentrated inside the large, heterogeneous areas that a single areal label cannot resolve. Where the two maps disagree, cyto7's label better matches the independent multimodal profile in 60.1% of pooled feature-by-vertex comparisons, against 46% under a rotation null and 54% under granularity-matched alternative partitions (p = 0.020), the harder of the two. A per-vertex anatomical support score, computed from anatomy alone, states how strongly each hand-drawn label is backed by the anatomical evidence, and is deliberately not a calibrated error probability. We then validate cyto7 against independent brain measures not used to define it, under a spatial-autocorrelation (spin) null with FDR control. Intracortical myelin (T1w/T2w) increases, cortical thickness decreases, and the principal functional-connectivity gradient reverses along the type axis (all q of about 0.006 or less). Source-reconstructed resting-state MEG dynamics also track the axis: the intrinsic timescale shortens toward koniocortex (rho of about -0.46) and survives the null, as do the spectral centroid and the slow/fast band-power ratio, whereas the aperiodic 1/f exponent does not. The laminar marker genes are where cyto7 differs most from a quantisation of a continuous map: it shows a larger absolute correlation with the layer-IV marker RORB (rho = +0.78) and the layer-V marker FEZF2 (-0.59) than seven-level septiles of myelin, of the functional gradient or of a histological gradient, on four of five markers, while tying or losing to those septiles on the macroscale proxies. These are larger observed associations against three tested quantisations, not a test that the differences between maps are reliable, and they do not establish the accuracy of any individual boundary. Defined from anatomy alone, cyto7 recovers the sensorimotor-to-association hierarchy and, on these markers, some of the laminar signal underlying it. It is released with its full pipeline and an uncalibrated anatomical support score as a reusable substrate for structure-function and modelling studies.

papers.title: Biophysical modeling of excitation/inhibition imbalance in Alzheimer's disease
papers.abstract: INTRODUCTION: Alzheimer's disease (AD) involves early sensory and perceptual changes that can precede memory decline. We developed a two-layer rate-based neural model of early and higher visual areas with feedforward, feedback, and recurrent connections to examine how excitatory/inhibitory (E/I) balance shapes visual motion perception in AD. METHODS: Using Motion-Induced Position Shift and Altered Motion Repulsion stimuli, we factorially manipulated excitatory (E) and inhibitory (I) subfield power and connectivity to examine their effects on illusion representation across visual layers. RESULTS: Increased E, decreased I, and increased E/I reduced illusion representation, consistent with reduced illusion susceptibility in AD, whereas the converse increased illusion representation, reflecting neurotypical processing. Higher-level layer 2 representations were more resistant to E/I perturbations than lower-level layer 1. Illusion representation was less affected by E/I increases in intra-areal (recurrent) connectivity than in inter-areal (feedforward/feedback) connectivity. DISCUSSION: This mechanistic framework links E/I balance and connectivity to altered visual motion illusion representations in AD and suggests that E/I and connectivity measures may provide probes of early AD neurobiology. The framework may also generalize beyond vision.

papers.title: Neural latent representation of implicit perceptual decision confidence signatures from brain-wide intracranial EEG
papers.abstract: Human perceptual decision confidence has been associated with brain-wide signalling, albeit with inconsistencies across studies. It remains unclear whether more robust neural latent representations exist, particularly for implicit confidence. We address this by applying complementary machine learning approaches to comprehensive, brain-wide intracranial electroencephalography (iEEG) data acquired without explicit confidence reports. Using explainable feature selection methods, we elucidated key spatiotemporal iEEG components, especially in the frontal cortex, that readily distinguished confidence characteristics related to decision correctness, difficulty, and speed, and that were transferable across motor modalities. Despite inconsistencies in the features identified across methods and conditions, dimensionality reductions revealed robust low-dimensional neural latent representations. Furthermore, their neural trajectories within a shared subspace enhanced the distinguishability of confidence characteristics. Overall, our results uncover low-dimensional spatial and temporal neural latent representations underlying human implicit perceptual decision confidence that are robust to analytical methods and decision conditions.

papers.title: Model-based pupil deconvolution reveals latent attentional dynamics
papers.abstract: Changes in pupil size have been widely used as an indirect measure of attention. However, attention engages on a faster timescale than the pupillary response. Therefore, the slow time course of the pupil response makes it difficult to distinguish attentional responses to stimuli presented in close temporal succession. Although signal deconvolution has been used in previous research to estimate latent attentional responses from the pupil signal, existing methods primarily model dilation without considering the visual stimulus evoked constriction phase of the pupil. Here, we introduce a dual-kernel deconvolution model that models constriction and dilation using separate impulse response functions. Using an RSVP paradigm with emotional faces as target stimuli, we demonstrate that the proposed model estimates latent attentional response despite substantial overlap in the measured pupil signal. Importantly, the recovered attentional response resembles the time course of attentional allocation previously predicted by several models of Attentional Blink. Together, these findings demonstrate that the dynamics of latent attentional episodes can be recovered from the pupil response with a temporal resolution previously obscured by the sluggishness of the pupillary response. The proposed method is also provided as a usable software package that serves as a general tool for investigating the temporal dynamics of attention in rapid visual paradigms.

papers.title: Associations Between Neural Responses to Social Fairness and Financial Exploitation Vulnerability Vary With Age and Emotional Intelligence
papers.abstract: Financial exploitation often arises in social contexts in which individuals must evaluate fairness, trust, and interpersonal information during financial decisions. We examined whether neural responses to fairness in social versus nonsocial contexts relate to financial exploitation vulnerability and whether these relationships vary with age, emotional intelligence, and affect. A total of 310 adults spanning ages 21-89 completed an fMRI Ultimatum Game in which they accepted or rejected offers from human and computer partners, along with measures of financial exploitation vulnerability, emotional intelligence, and affect. Participants were strongly sensitive to offer fairness, and individual differences in behavioral sensitivity to partner type were associated with social-relative anterior insula responses to unfairness. Greater baseline negative affect was associated with stronger anterior insula differentiation between social and nonsocial fairness. Financial exploitation vulnerability was associated with prefrontal responses to social-relative fairness in ways that depended on individual characteristics: age moderated its association with dorsomedial prefrontal cortex activation, whereas emotional intelligence moderated its association with dorsolateral prefrontal cortex activation. Whole-brain connectivity analyses further showed that age moderated associations between emotional intelligence and executive control network connectivity with posterior cingulate and right temporoparietal regions. These findings suggest that vulnerability to financial exploitation is reflected in how social context is integrated with affective and individual characteristics across adulthood.

papers.title: Auditory and visual mismatch negativity responses to numerical and non-numerical magnitudes in adults

topics.name: Cognitive and developmental aspects of mathematical skills

papers.abstract:
We investigated how auditory and visual presentation of small numerical magnitudes and non- numerical magnitudes are passively processed at the neural level. Earlier research suggests automatic processing of quantities occurs rapidly in the brain. However, there are no studies on passive, pre-attentive change detection of magnitudes utilizing mismatch negativity (MMN) across sensory modalities in same participants, important to understand amodal processing of magnitudes. We recorded EEG in passive auditory and visual multi-feature oddball and control paradigms from the same adult individuals (N=104/105, respectively). In the auditory paradigm, the standard stimulus was a 2-part sound, while the deviant stimuli varied in frequency, intensity, gap length, and number of sounds (1-part and 3-part stimuli). In the visual paradigm, the standard stimulus was a dot array containing two medium-sized dots, while the deviant stimuli varied in numerosity (1 or 3 dots) and dot size (small or large).

The results for the auditory paradigm showed significant MMN across all features, including comparisons with deviant-alone control stimuli, except for the 2-part vs. 1-part contrast. The results for the visual paradigm suggested differences in processing across all features apart from large and medium-size stimuli. These results replicate earlier MMN findings that the brain distinguishes pre-attentively changes in sound frequency, amplitude and gap. Auditorily presented small numerical magnitudes also showed pre-attentive processing but less robustly to the contrast 2 vs. 1. Visual pre-attentive processing of small numerical magnitudes was also observed. Together these findings could be interpreted to support the existence of abstract, pre- attentive processing of numerical magnitudes.

Highlights* Auditory and visual processing of numerical and non-numerical magnitudes was examined with EEG

* Auditory non-numerical magnitudes and medium vs. small dots replicated earlier MMN studies

* aMMN and vMMN showed pre-attentive processing of changes in small numerosities 2 vs. 3 and 2 vs. 1

* 2 vs. 1 tone processing was less robust than 2 vs. 3 or the processing of the visual contrasts

* The brain processes changes in small non-symbolic magnitudes pre-attentively
