papers.title: Age-related differences in episodic memory precision are robust across time of day, chronotype, and testing format
papers.abstract:
Older adults typically exhibit reduced episodic memory precision, while maintaining relatively preserved retrieval success. However, little is known about whether these age-related differences are influenced by internal biological factors (e.g., chronotype) or external testing conditions (e.g., experiment format, time of day).

To address this question, younger and older adults completed an object-location memory task online, either in the morning or evening, and either with or without video-based supervision. Memory performance was assessed using mean absolute error and Bayesian hierarchical mixture modelling, which dissociated memory precision ({kappa}) from the probability of memory-based responding ({theta}).

Immediate memory performance was high across age groups, irrespective of time of day. Greater encoding error predicted greater retrieval error, and participants tested in the video condition exhibited lower recall error and higher recognition performance than those tested without supervision. Consistent with prior studies, older adults exhibited reduced memory precision relative to younger adults, whereas retrieval success remained largely intact. However, Bayesian Hierarchical Modelling provided no evidence that time of day, experiment format, or their interactions with age influenced either memory precision or retrieval probability. Older adults reported stronger morning preferences than younger adults, and participants generally selected testing times that aligned with their chronotype. Nevertheless, alignment between chronotype and testing time did not modulate memory performance. The results indicate that age-related differences in episodic memory precision are robust across variations in testing context, including time of day, experiment format, and individual differences in chronotype.

More broadly, the results support the feasibility of remote and unsupervised testing for memory precision research and suggest that chronotype and testing time are unlikely to be major sources of variability in immediate object-location memory performance.

papers.title: Median Preoptic Brs3-Expressing Neurons Regulate Heat-Evoked Defensive Escalation
papers.abstract: Animals confronted with increasing heat must switch from exploratory behavior to vigorous actions that limit further exposure, but the forebrain circuits controlling this transition are poorly understood. We exposed male mice to progressively stronger floor heating while providing continuous access to a climbing mesh separated from the heating plate. Higher plate settings shifted behavior from rearing toward wall-directed digging and climbing, with jumping at the highest setting, and increased c-Fos labeling in the median preoptic nucleus. Neurons expressing bombesin receptor subtype 3 showed greater c-Fos recruitment under strong heating, and their population calcium signals increased when mice entered the plate-controlled zone and decreased when they left. Optogenetic activation without heating produced place avoidance, vigorous actions, and increased locomotion. Inhibition reduced locomotion and, during strong heating, shifted behavior from climbing and jumping toward rearing and weakened avoidance of a localized heat source. These findings identify median preoptic Brs3-expressing neurons as regulators of behavioral escalation and heat avoidance.

papers.title: Exacerbation of neurodegeneration by a metabolically engineered bacterium in a mouse model of tauopathy
papers.abstract:
BackgroundTherapeutics that modulate peripheral and central immune responses are emerging as promising approaches for neurodegenerative disease. However, the biological context in which these interventions are deployed may critically influence therapeutic outcomes. An attenuated Brucella melitensis 16M strain and a similar strain engineered to express the metabolite indole have previously demonstrated therapeutic efficacy in preclinical models of cancer and autoimmunity through immune system modulation. Here, we tested whether repeated administration of these bacterial strains could modify pathological outcomes in a mouse model of tauopathy.

MethodsAttenuated Brucella strains were administered to transgenic mice overexpressing mutant tau protein on a human APOE4 knock-in background via intraperitoneal injection every 5 weeks starting at 6 months of age. Mice were analyzed at 9.5 months of age for tau pathology, neurodegeneration, and changes in innate and adaptive immune responses.

ResultsBrucella strains distributed predominantly in the periphery following repeated intraperitoneal treatment in transgenic mice, with minimal detection in the brain and no detection in the dural meninges. Repeated administration of either bacterial strain was well tolerated, with no evidence of adverse safety events. Surprisingly, repeated treatment with the engineered Brucella strain exacerbated neurodegenerative pathology, resulting in reduced hippocampal volume and increased phosphorylated tau pathology compared with control- and non-engineered Brucella strain -treated animals. Immunohistochemical analyses revealed increased numbers of hippocampal CD4+ T cells following treatment with either Brucella strain relative to PBS controls. However, only treatment with the engineered Brucella increased microglial reactivity within the hippocampus.

ConclusionThese findings demonstrate that peripheral administration of an engineered bacterial therapeutic can differentially influence neuroimmune responses and disease progression. These results underscore the importance of disease context when developing bacteria-based immunomodulatory therapies for neurodegenerative disorders.

papers.title: Biphasic Modulation of Absence Seizures by Lisuride in GAERS: Dissecting the Role of 5-HT2A Receptors
papers.abstract:
BackgroundSerotonergic signaling plays an important role in the modulation of absence seizures (ASs), and activation of serotonin 2A receptors (5-HT2ARs) with TCB-2 suppresses spontaneous absence seizures (ASs) in Genetic Absence Epilepsy Rats from Strasbourg (GAERS). Lisuride is a pharmacologically complex serotonergic and dopaminergic ligand with low 5-HT2AR signaling efficacy and a receptor profile distinct from that of TCB-2. We therefore investigated its effects on spontaneous ASs and the contribution of 5-HT2ARs to its actions.

MethodsThe effects of systemic lisuride (0.1 and 0.5 mg/kg) on spontaneous ASs were examined in freely moving GAERS over 120 min by quantifying time spent in seizure, mean seizure duration and seizure number. The contribution of 5-HT2ARs was investigated by administering lisuride (0.5 mg/kg) following pretreatment with the selective 5-HT2AR antagonist MDL11,939 (0.5 mg/kg).

ResultsLisuride produced marked dose- and time-dependent effects on ASs. At 0.1 mg/kg, lisuride elicited modest pro-absence effect. In contrast, 0.5 mg/kg produced a pronounced biphasic response, with a marked reduction in seizure activity during the first 40 min, followed by rebound increase during the second hour. The early suppression involved reductions in both seizure number and duration, whereas the delayed pro-absence effect was predominantly associated with prolonged ASs. MDL11,939 did not prevent the early seizure suppression but blocked the increase in seizure duration while producing a transient increase in seizure number.

ConclusionsLisuride is a dose- and time-dependent bidirectional modulator of ASs in GAERS. The persistence of the profound early anti-absence effect during 5-HT2AR blockade indicates that this response does not require 5-HT2AR activation, whereas the modification of the delayed response by MDL11,939 supports a 5-HT2AR-dependent component in the later phase. These findings distinguish lisuride pharmacologically from TCB-2 and suggest that its biphasic effects arise from the dynamic engagement of multiple receptor mechanisms, potentially including dopaminergic signaling.

papers.title: Scale-mixture Langevin sampling in the subspaces of recurrent cortical circuit dynamics
papers.abstract: Recurrent cortical circuits are hypothesized to perform Bayesian posterior sampling through their stochastic dynamics. Yet identifying which sampling algorithm a circuit intrinsically implements, as opposed to mapping manually designing algorithms onto circuits, requires rigorous theoretical analysis of the biological circuit dynamics, and remains a fundamental open challenge because of the analytical intractability of nonlinear recurrent dynamics. Here, we tackle this challenge through comprehensive theoretical analysis of analytically tractable nonlinear recurrent circuit dynamics used in neuroscience research-- the continuous attractor network (CAN). Surprisingly, we find that the circuit, without any non-Gaussian components in its connectivity or internal variability, intrinsically emerges heavy-tailed subspaces dynamics described as scale-mixture Langevin posterior sampling. The mechanism emerges from the circuits own nonlinear dynamics: divisive normalization renders the overall population activation Gamma-distributed which multiplicatively modulates the time constant of the Langevin sampling in the stimulus feature subspace. Eventually, this scale-mixture structure produces a heavy-tailed (Student-t) sampling step size distribution, significantly accelerating the sampling speed. Moreover, the scale-mixture Langevin sampling approaches a Levy-like regime in the weak input limit. Our results analytically identify an intrinsic circuit algorithm embedded in subspaces of nonlinear recurrent dynamics, and establish a minimal circuit mechanism for endogenous heavy-tail statistics without any explicit non-Gaussian components.

papers.title: Genetically distinct neurodegenerative proteinopathies engage overlapping proteostasis components
papers.abstract: Neurodegenerative proteinopathies are defined by distinct proteins whose folding, trafficking and clearance depend on shared proteostasis machinery. Whether these disorders engage common components or only common processes has been unresolved. We mapped 16 disease proteins from 12 disorders onto a fixed 990-protein proteostasis network. Across the 12 disorders, the neighborhoods of these proteins shared specific proteins beyond expectations from process composition and connectivity. The same held for the two disorders defined by more than one protein. Nine proteins contributed disproportionately, and only autophagys removal significantly reduced similarity. Removing PRKN, HSPA8 or UBQLN2 in silico reduced path efficiency, marking them candidate shared network vulnerabilities. In human brain proteomes, Alzheimers disease-zone proteins showed greater abundance remodeling in the insoluble fraction; recurrence across disorders showed no such association. The result is a component-level architecture prioritizing network-derived candidates for cross-disease functional testing.

papers.title: The olfactory ventricle: an overlooked and evolutionarily conserved feature of the mammalian brain
papers.abstract: The olfactory ventricle (OV), an anterior extension of the lateral ventricular system into the olfactory bulbs, is generally considered a transient developmental structure that closes during early postnatal life. However, this view largely derives from a limited number of laboratory models, and the evolutionary distribution and cellular organization of the adult OV remain poorly understood. Here, we combined a comparative survey of mammalian neuroanatomy with phylogenetic analyses and cellular characterization of the OV across species. We compiled anatomical data for 154 mammalian species spanning 26 orders and 80 families, revealing widespread persistence of a patent OV into adulthood. Phylogenetic analyses supported OV presence as the ancestral mammalian state and indicated that its absence is phylogenetically structured and consistent with repeated secondary losses. Chiroptera displayed multiple lineage-specific losses, whereas variation within Muridae extended to the intraspecific level, with contrasting OV persistence among Mus musculus and Rattus norvegicus populations. Comparative histological analyses in sheep, Peromyscus maniculatus, and CD1 mice revealed that, despite marked interspecific differences in OV morphology, the persistent ventricular region retains a conserved cellular organization characterized by progenitor- and glial-associated markers, proliferative cells, immature neuronal populations, and a differentiated apical/ciliary interface. Although these observations do not establish local neuronal production or demonstrate that the OV constitutes an autonomous neurogenic niche, their convergence across species indicates that the persistent adult OV is not simply an anatomically residual lumen but a specialized component of mammalian olfactory bulb organization. Together, our findings identify the OV as an ancestral and widely conserved feature of the mammalian brain and provide an evolutionary and cellular framework for investigating the developmental mechanisms controlling its persistence and its potential contribution to adult olfactory neurogenesis and plasticity.

papers.title: Multiscale structural MRI differences among collegiate American football players, cross-country runners, and non-athletes
papers.abstract: Structural differences observed in collision-sport athletes may reflect repetitive head-impact exposure, broader effects of athletic training, or pre-existing individual variation, making inclusion of a non-collision athlete group important for interpretation of any differences seen. Here, structural T1-weighted MRI data from 17 collegiate American football players, 16 cross-country runners, and 9 non-athletes were analyzed using FSL voxel-based morphometry (VBM), FIRST subcortical volumetry and vertex-wise shape analysis, and FAST whole-brain tissue segmentation. Spatial inference used permutation testing with threshold-free cluster enhancement and family-wise error correction, while scalar analyses used multiplicity-corrected procedures. FAST-derived absolute tissue volumes were also examined in a sensitivity analysis adjusting for FreeSurfer estimated total intracranial volume (eTIV). VBM showed recurrent brainstem-centered differences, with non-athletes showing greater local gray matter measures than both athlete groups, whereas football players showed greater brainstem measures than runners. FIRST vertex-wise analysis identified corrected differences involving the brainstem and selected subcortical structures, while no total FIRST structure volume survived false discovery rate correction. Unadjusted FAST analysis identified a CSF group effect, F(2, 24.38) = 11.46, p < .001, q = .001. After eTIV adjustment, the CSF group effect remained, F(2, 38) = 14.30, q < .001, and a white matter group effect was also identified, F(2, 38) = 9.59, q < .001; gray matter and total segmented tissue did not show corrected adjusted effects. papers.title: Hypothalamic tauP301L pathology disrupts pair bonding in monogamous prairie voles
papers.abstract: Although dementias primarily affect memory, they also disrupt our closest social relationships, resulting in elevated caregiver burden and worse patient outcomes. However, the mechanistic study of how pathology affects social attachments is limited by the use of laboratory rodents that do not form selective, long-term bonds. Here, in monogamous prairie voles, we expressed dementia-causing tauP301L in the paraventricular hypothalamus of 12- and 18-month-old animals, and separately, from birth through 18-months, across hippocampocortical regions. Hippocampocortical expression of tauP301L did not yield deficits in social or non-social dementia-related phenotypes. In contrast, tauP301L expressed in the hypothalamus yielded sex- and age-dependent social bonding deficits. 18-month males with hypothalamic tau pathology failed to form bonds and displayed blunted sociability, effects that converged across bonding assays. In addition, healthy 18-month males paired with a hypothalamic tau-expressing female also showed reduced partner preference, suggesting that pathology exerts vicarious effects on partners. Social behavior of both healthy females and those expressing tauP301L were unaffected. 18-month tauP301L males also showed elevated oxytocin fluorescence. These findings establish direct and vicarious disruptions to pair bonding induced by hypothalamic tau pathology in male prairie voles, potentially via altered oxytocin signaling.

papers.title: A shared circuit architecture for multiscale signal recognition in crickets
papers.abstract: Communication signals often contain behaviorally relevant structure on multiple temporal scales. Short-timescale features are commonly thought to be recognized first and then integrated into longer-timescale representations. Whether a shared circuit can instead recognize multiple timescales remains unclear. Cricket calling songs provide a tractable test because millisecond-scale pulses are grouped into chirps lasting hundreds of milliseconds. We combined female phonotaxis with a mechanistic model of the identified pulse-recognition network to ask whether this circuitry can also generate chirp selectivity. In Gryllus bimaculatus, the model, originally parameterized from pulse-scale electrophysiology and behavior, recovered the main boundaries of chirp preference without fitting to chirp behavior. Coincidence detection generated the minimum chirp-duration requirement, whereas suppressive computations in the networks input neuron shaped the upper boundaries for chirp duty cycle and period. Across 14 species, varying these suppressive computations captured major differences in chirp tuning. These findings reveal a temporally interleaved serial circuit in which long-timescale selectivity begins upstream of completed short-timescale selectivity, offering an alternative to both conventional short-first hierarchies and parallel pathways.

papers.title: Causal event structure shapes convergent reactivation signatures in human cortex and language model
papers.abstract: Humans adapt to changing environments by understanding the latent causal structure of events, and modern large language models (LLMs) increasingly exhibit analogous abilities. However, elucidating how causal knowledge is represented and integrated in the human brain and in LLMs poses a substantial challenge for cognitive science. To address this, we combine topological analysis of representational manifolds with neuroscientific analyses of reactivation. We find that event-level causal relations modulate temporally structured neural reactivation in the human brain, particularly in the angular gyrus, precuneus and prefrontal cortex. By contrast, LLMs express these relations through positionally structured representational reactivation. Despite these differences, the resulting reactivation patterns exhibit similar intrinsic manifold structure across the two systems. Together, these findings suggest that the human brain and LLM share a common principle for organizing causal knowledge.

papers.title: Single-cell spatial transcriptomics of inherited retinal degeneration reveals broad and focal organization of disease responses
papers.abstract: Inherited retinal degenerations are largely monogenic disorders characterized by progressive photoreceptor dysfunction and death. Although the transcriptomic responses to inherited degeneration are well-characterized, how these responses are spatially organized across the retinal axis has not been mapped. Here, we used seqFISH to spatially profile 173 cell identity and degeneration-associated genes with single-cell, single-transcript resolution in male wild-type and LCA5gt/gtmouse retinas at early, intermediate, and advanced disease stages. In early disease, rod injury and stress response markers were enriched in the superior retina, while rod function and identity markers were enriched in the inferior retina. Nested within the broader superior-inferior organization, a coordinated rod injury response comprising Edn2, Fgf2, Socs3, and Stat3 was organized into focal regions on the order of 100 m in width, with high-response regions directly adjacent to low-response regions. These focal regions were locally enriched for markers of Muller reactive gliosis and rod stress responses. Our single-cell spatiotemporal map reveals that transcriptional responses to degeneration vary at both the broad and focal scales, and offers a framework for investigating how local tissue properties and interactions among neighboring cells may contribute to disease progression.

papers.title: High-throughput serial two-photon tomography with BakingTray and BrainSaw
papers.abstract: Volumetric imaging is increasingly important in fields such as neuroscience, where quantifying structure and mapping features are inherently three-dimensional problems. Block-face serial two-photon tomography (STPT) has emerged as a powerful approach for high-resolution, whole-organ volumetric imaging. STPT avoids complex sample preparation and balances image quality, speed, and scalability. However, STPT remains niche, in part because of the absence of flexible, general-purpose control software. Here we present BakingTray, an open-source software platform for STPT that extends ScanImage. BakingTrays modular framework accommodates diverse hardware configurations and allows users to build systems customised to their needs. Twelve such systems, which we call  BrainSaws, have been constructed worldwide since 2016, with more under construction, and have so far contributed to 35 research papers. The three systems at the Sainsbury Wellcome Centre alone have acquired over 7,000 samples in a busy multi-user facility. We demonstrate the platform across its core neuroscience applications: electrode track localisation, brain-wide cell counting, and bulk projection mapping. Beyond these, we map the cell-type-specific synaptic output of inhibitory neurons in the ventral lateral geniculate nucleus and, with whole-mount staining, amyloid plaques brain-wide in a mouse model of Alzheimers disease. BakingTray is a mature platform for groups or facilities needing a customised volumetric imaging solution, whether built new or converted cheaply from an existing two-photon microscope.

papers.title: Thalamic Dysconnectivity and Negative Symptoms in Schizophrenia Spectrum Disorder
papers.abstract: Background and Hypothesis Negative symptoms in schizophrenia spectrum disorder (SSD) are associated with poor functional outcomes and reduced quality of life; however, effective treatments remain limited. A better understanding of the underlying brain mechanisms is needed to develop better treatments. Neuroimaging studies implicate multiple brain networks in negative symptoms, though findings remain heterogeneous, potentially reflecting the multidimensionality of both symptoms and brain networks. Larger, more systematic dissections are required to identify the key hub(s) underlying negative symptoms. Study Design Structural MRI data from 394 participants (210 SSD, 184 healthy controls [HC]) were analyzed to identify cortical thickness and subcortical volume demonstrating both SSD-HC differences and associations with negative symptoms measured by the Brief Negative Symptom Scale (BNSS). Regions meeting both criteria were selected as seeds for resting-state functional connectivity analyses in 143 SSD patients to examine association with negative symptoms and their subdomains. Study Results The thalamus was the only region demonstrating significant structural abnormalities both in SSD and an association with BNSS total score (p-FDR<0.05). Functional-network-defined thalamic subregions were subsequently examined. Several thalamic hypoconnectivities were significantly corresponded with negative symptoms, involving thalamic subregions associated with the cortical default mode, somatosensory, medial temporal, and dorsal attention networks (p=0.001, corrected<0.05). Blunted affect showed the most extensive thalamic connectivity alterations, involving the striatum, cerebellum, and temporoparietal junction/superior temporal sulcus (TPJ-STS). Thalamic hypoconnectivity with TPJ-STS was also associated with overall negative symptoms and anhedonia. Conclusions This study identifies the thalamus as a central hub of negative symptom-related dysfunction in SSD and highlights specific thalamic subnetworks as potential targets for circuit-based interventions.

topics.name: Effects and risks of endocrine disrupting chemicals

papers.title: On-demand surround suppression explains the spatiotemporal window of the tilt illusion
papers.abstract: What we see at one location depends on what surrounds it. Such contextual effects are thought to arise from neural signals that travel across the retinotopic representations. Because these signals need more time to travel longer distances, a more distant surround should influence perception most strongly when presented earlier, compensating for its delay. We tested this prediction in human observers using a visual illusion in which a central target appears tilted away from the orientation of its surround (tilt illusion). Measuring the temporal window of this illusion using psychophysical reverse correlation revealed the opposite: the most effective surround occurred progressively later as distance increased. Computational modelling demonstrated that this reversal is explained if the visual system sends out a query that recruits contextual information on demand. Perceptual appearance may thus be constructed through temporally unfolding interactions in which context is actively gathered, not passively received.

papers.title: Resolution-aware spectral parameterization reveals robust context-dependent aperiodic EEG dynamics during real-world table tennis
papers.abstract: Mobile EEG can link neuroimaging to natural behavior, but effects recorded during movement, and sport in particular, are difficult to interpret because neural activity overlaps with signals from movement, muscle activity, and cable movement artifacts. We analyzed the OpenNeuro Real World Table Tennis dataset to test whether peri-hit spectral activity could be analyzed and how it differed between human-opponent and ball-machine play. Data from 25 participants comprising EEG, noise-layers, EMG and motion recordings was analyzed with pre-hit, impact, and post-hit windows. EEG power bands were residualized using trial-level root mean square from noise-layer, EMG, and motion/miscellaneous channels. Spectral parameterization modeled spectra as an aperiodic component plus periodic peaks. The principal short-window model was resolution-aware; sensitivity analyses reduced model complexity, used a 2.0-s peri-hit subwindow (-1.0 to +1.0 s), or disabled periodic fitting. Results showed residualized alpha and beta power was lower during ball-machine play, including pre-hit posterior alpha power. The clearest context difference was a higher ball-machine aperiodic exponent over posterior and parietal sensors, corresponding to a steeper broadband spectral slope. Posterior post-hit means were 0.451 and 0.606 for human-opponent and ball-machine play, respectively. A focal parietal effect persisted across specifications. The results support artifact-informed, resolution-aware spectral analysis as an effective approach for detecting robust spectral differences between naturalistic visuomotor contexts and suggest that EEG may provide useful information about the processes engaged by different practice environments, without establishing a single cognitive or physiological mechanism or demonstrating a training outcome.

papers.title: A psychophysical characterization of tactile and temperature perception on the human torso
papers.abstract: Numerous studies have been conducted to investigate touch on the hand and forearm, but less is known about the rest of the body, particularly the torso and breasts, which play an important role in affective touch. We conducted psychophysical tests on three skin sites on the torso: upper breast, nipple-areola complex (NAC), and under the breast, as well as on two control sites: palm and forearm. We studied touch pleasantness and intensity by applying gentle caress-like strokes using a soft brush, and measured temperature and tactile detection thresholds. The results show an inverted U-shaped relationship for pleasantness over increasing stroking velocity for all skin sites, although we found some differences between sites, particularly at 30 cm.s-1, where participants found stroking on the NAC to be more intense and women additionally found it to be less pleasant. For temperature detection, we found that the NAC was more sensitive in men. For tactile detection, we mainly observed that the areola was far less sensitive than the other areas. Together, these results provide insights into tactile perception in the torso on a fundamental level, which can be applied to understanding how to regain sensations after mastectomy.

papers.title: Wavelet Transform Coherence Under Controlled Temporal Correspondence and Social Co-Presence: Implications for fNIRS Hyperscanning
papers.abstract: Interpersonal neural synchrony research using functional near-infrared spectroscopy (fNIRS) frequently relies on wavelet transform coherence (WTC) to quantify temporal correspondence between cortical signals. Yet, whether WTC reliably recovers experimentally defined differences in signal correspondence remains insufficiently established. Here, we evaluated WTC using an auditory-guided finger-tapping paradigm in which matching and non-matching temporal structures were compared within participants and between dyad members during individual and joint performance. Task-evoked analyses confirmed reliable recruitment of contralateral motor and premotor regions across both contexts, whereas the ipsilateral motor cortex was significantly recruited only during joint performance and was the only region differing between sessions. WTC sensitivity was strongly modulated by social co-presence. Within participants, WTC failed to discriminate matching from non-matching temporal structures during individual performance, whereas robust matching-related increases emerged during joint performance, particularly in contralateral motor and premotor regions. Between participants, WTC showed limited and region-specific discrimination when participants were tested separately, but higher coherence for matching temporal structures emerged during joint performance, particularly in motor regions. These findings show that WTC can recover experimentally defined temporal correspondence between fNIRS signals, but that this sensitivity is not context-independent. The within-participant results further suggest that social co-presence may alter the temporal dynamics of the individual neural signals themselves. WTC should therefore be interpreted as a context-sensitive measure whose meaning depends on the functional and social processes generating the signals being compared.

papers.title: SAIL: Sparse Autoencoders for Interpretable Alignment of Human Vision and Multimodal Large Language Models
papers.abstract: Alignment between human high-level visual representations and those of multimodal large language models (MLLMs) offers a quantitative framework for understanding information processing in human vision. However, similarities between model and brain representations do not directly reveal the semantic content underlying their correspondence, as this content is difficult to isolate in entangled MLLM representations. Here, we introduce SAIL, an interpretable framework that formulates voxel interpretation as a multi-unit sparse semantic correspondence problem between MLLMs and human vision. First, we train unified cross-layer sparse autoencoders (SAEs) on MLLM representations of Natural Scenes Dataset images and captions, and align each brain voxel with multiple SAE units. Second, we quantify semantic similarity between their top-response image sets to map semantic alignment across the cortex. We project multiple semantic labels back onto the cortex to interpret the content of this alignment. Finally, we assess these correspondences using category responses measured in independent fLoc experiments. Compared with SAEs trained independently at each layer, SAIL exhibits lower redundancy in SAE unit response profiles and higher semantic alignment. We find that semantic alignment is organized along the human ventral visual pathway across the models and subjects examined. The projected labels reveal semantic preferences within canonical visual regions, while fLoc experiments show agreement between predicted and measured category response patterns. Exploratory analyses further reveal cortical distributions of action-related semantics consistent with established functional accounts of lateral occipitotemporal and posterior parietal cortex. Overall, SAIL provides an interpretable account of the semantic correspondences between MLLM representations and human visual responses.

papers.title: Netrin signaling shapes sexually dimorphic neurite branching of a sex-shared interneuron in C. elegans
papers.abstract: Sexually dimorphic behaviors arise from underlying differences in neural circuit architecture between the sexes, yet the molecular mechanisms that establish these structural differences remain poorly understood. In Caenorhabditis elegans, the sex-shared interneuron AVG exhibits sexually dimorphic synaptic connectivity, offering a model for investigating the development of sexually dimorphic neuronal morphology. Here, we identified that AVG displays male-specific neurite branching and demonstrated that the conserved axon guidance cue UNC-6/Netrin and its receptor UNC-40/DCC are essential for this structural remodeling. Cell-specific manipulation of sexual identity revealed that male identity confers branching competence to AVG. Loss of UNC-6 or UNC-40 abolished branch formation, whereas loss of the alternate Netrin receptor UNC-5/Unc5 had no detectable effect. Cell-specific rescue experiments showed that UNC-40 functions in AVG through its UNC-6 binding domains. Furthermore, genetic ablation of the male-specific presynaptic neuron PCA, which expresses unc-6, diminished AVG branch length, establishing PCA as a candidate local source of UNC-6. Together, our findings support a model in which presynaptic UNC-6/Netrin cues from male-specific neurons promote dimorphic neurite branching in sex-shared neurons, illustrating how evolutionarily conserved signaling molecules are redeployed during sexual maturation to sculpt sex-specific neural circuits.

papers.title: A comprehensive physiological dataset of pain and aversive modalities for pain biomarkers research
papers.abstract: While progress has been made in identifying pain biomarkers using neuroimaging, the development of reliable EEG-based biomarkers remains challenging, limited by small sample sizes and the lack of adequate control conditions. We present a comprehensive dataset from 125 pain-free adults, comprising electroencephalogram (EEG) recordings, and behavioural, sociodemographic, and psychological data. Galvanic skin response and electrocardiogram data were also recorded in a subset of participants (n = 76). Participants received two sustained painful stimulations (thermal, chemical) and two sustained aversive non-painful stimulations (auditory, taste), each delivered twice (with and without continuous intensity ratings). Data are provided in Brain Imaging Data Structure format, where all physiological, stimulus-related, and behavioural data are synchronized within the EEG data files for easy access and analysis. Technical validation confirmed data integrity, with spectral and physiological analyses showing responses associated with stimulus intensity and subjective pain/unpleasantness levels. By providing multimodal physiological data across painful and non-painful aversive conditions, this initiative represents a valuable resource for developing or validating biomarkers and exploring the multidimensional nature of pain perception.

papers.title: Axonal dysfunction precedes axonal degeneration in a mouse model of progressive parkinsonism
papers.abstract: Axons of substantia nigra dopaminergic neurons "die back" in Parkinson's disease (PD), exhibiting early degeneration relative to cell bodies, a key feature also observed in PD models. A critical step towards understanding the process of axonal neurodegeneration is to determine the physiological properties of dopaminergic axons that are altered during the early stages of cellular dysfunction. Here, we compared the electrophysiology and calcium dynamics of dopaminergic axons in the MitoPark model of PD with age-matched controls. Our experiments show a pronounced reduction in action potential (AP)-evoked calcium signals in MitoPark axons that emerges well before the onset of dopaminergic fiber loss and motor deficits. In addition, calcium imaging and direct axon recording revealed deficits in AP propagation accompanied by alterations in the axonal AP waveform. Therefore, our experimental findings identify the progression of axon-specific physiological deficits that occur long before neurodegeneration, more precisely defining the period that precedes axonal loss.

papers.title: The potato cyst nematode Globodera pallida possesses an expanded serotonergic nervous system
papers.abstract: Abstract The neurotransmitter serotonin (5-hydroxytryptamine; 5-HT) controls behaviours that are essential for the parasitic lifestyle of plant parasitic nematodes (PPNs). Here, we used serotonin immunochemistry and in situ hybridization for the serotonin synthesis genes, Gpa-tph-1 and Gpa-bas-1, to map its signalling pathways in Globodera pallida J2 infective stages. We identified fourteen serotonin-immunoreactive cell bodies around the pharyngeal median bulb and revealed that eleven of them co-express Gpa-tph-1 and Gpa-bas-1, confirming these are serotonin-synthesising neurons. Serotonin immunoreactivity was also localised in structures consistent with labelling of amphids, and in sixteen non-neuronal cells located in the middle and posterior region of the nematode. Depletion of serotonin with reserpine reduced the serotonin immunoreactivity in all fourteen cell bodies confirming their neuronal identity, but not in non-neuronal tissue. We identified additional, but infrequent expression of Gpa-tph-1 in two cells and expression of Gpa-bas-1 in one pair of symmetrically bilateral cells anterior to the median bulb, that lacked serotonin immunoreactivity. The results reveal distinct pools of serotonin distribution in G. pallida and indicate serotonin signalling is more complex than in other parasitic nematodes and C. elegans, highlighting evolutionary divergence in neurotransmitter identity.

papers.title: The Walking Brain: Mapping feature-specific cortical responses to naturally unfolding sensory experience in the real world
papers.abstract: Understanding how the brain processes the everyday world is fundamental, yet laboratory paradigms exclude self-generated movement, unscripted events, and a continuously evolving multisensory environment. Wearable neuroimaging enables real-world measurement, but linking neural activity to uncontrolled sensory information remains challenging. Here, we extend a feature-based framework from naturalistic movie viewing to everyday behavior using wearable whole-head high-density fNIRS and participant-specific audiovisual recordings during movies and outdoor walking with no explicit task or scripted audiovisual sequence. Luminance- and sound-related cortical maps showed significant spatial correspondence, particularly in visual and auditory regions, whereas face-related correspondence was weaker. Luminance- and face-related maps were reproducible within individuals across repeated walks. Additional exploratory analysis demonstrated, to our knowledge, the first out-of-sample encoding of continuous environmental features during unconstrained real-world fNIRS, predicting cortical activity during held-out walking periods. Together, these findings establish a feature-based framework for linking cortical activity to naturally unfolding sensory experience in everyday behavior.

papers.title: Facial color properties affect perceived age.
papers.abstract: Age is a fundamental social attribute that affects rights, responsibilities and even social status. Color information of the face can affect perceived age, but the nature of its contribution, independent of luminance information, remains underexplored. To better characterize the role of color in age perception, we conducted two experiments. In our first experiment, we tested whether natural age-related changes in facial color alone can drive changes in perceived age. In our second experiment, we manipulated red-green contrast across faces aged 18-91 and tested the effect of this manipulation of perceived youthfulness. Our findings demonstrate that natural age-related color changes do provide cues for age perception, dissociable from luminance information. We also found that the optimal red-green contrast level to make faces look the youngest was significantly higher than the originals, meaning that faces tended to appear younger when their redness was accentuated, even though average face redness increases with age. Our analysis revealed that younger faces required greater increases in redness level compared to their older counterparts to achieve the youngest appearance. These results suggest that the spatial distribution of redness contributes to apparent youthfulness, especially in younger faces.

papers.title: Templated seeding induces the formation of Alzheimer paired helical tau filaments in human brain organoids
papers.abstract: The prion concept postulates that seeded aggregation results in the recruitment of soluble protein monomers and their assembly into amyloid filaments with the same structures as those of the seeds. Here we show that this concept applies to tau filaments formed in cortical organoids obtained from human iPSCs of control subjects. Tau seeds were extracted from the frontal cortex of individuals with Alzheimer disease. When added to human cortical organoids expressing endogenous levels of three-repeat tau, they gave rise to filaments of three-repeat tau whose formation required endogenous tau expression. By cryo-EM, these seeded tau filaments were identical to the paired helical filaments of the seeds. This novel finding demonstrates the faithful templated seeding of tau in human nerve cells expressing endogenous levels of tau and opens the way to studying the mechanisms of paired helical filament formation and their downstream effects in a human system amenable to genetic modification.

papers.title: Templated paired helical filament formation and tau fold-dependent inclusion morphologies in primary neurons
papers.abstract: Neurodegenerative tauopathies are characterized by the abnormal assembly of tau into amyloid filaments with distinct, disease-specific folds. These filaments are proposed to spread in a prion-like manner, thus underlying the progression of pathology in diseased brains. A prediction of this hypothesis is that tau filaments will induce progeny filaments identical to the input seed material, yet cellular models of templated tau assembly have failed to fully recapitulate brain-derived filament structures. Here, we show that mixed primary mouse cortical neurons overexpressing full-length human tau via adeno-associated virus transduction propagate Alzheimer's disease paired helical filaments upon exposure to human brain-derived seeds. Using minimal tags and core mutations, we were able to unambiguously differentiate induced aggregates from the original seeds. Super-resolution microscopy and live-cell imaging revealed progressive inclusion formation in neurons. Moreover, seeding primary neurons with brain extracts from individuals with Pick's disease, corticobasal degeneration and progressive supranuclear palsy induced the formation of morphologically distinct inclusions. Together, these findings establish that primary neurons provide an environment for the faithful propagation of paired helical filaments and show that tau filament folds dictate higher-order inclusion morphologies within neurons.

papers.title: Shared Fine-Scale Functional Organization in the Human Subcortex Revealed by Connectivity Hyperalignment
papers.abstract: Subcortical structures are central to cognition, emotion, and social processing, and their dysfunction underlies a wide range of neurological and psychiatric conditions. Yet subcortical fine-scale functional organization has remained largely inaccessible to group-level fMRI analysis: nuclei are small and low-SNR, and their functional topography varies idiosyncratically across individuals in ways that anatomical alignment cannot resolve. This idiosyncrasy carries real stakes. For example, deep brain stimulation targets with more variable functional connectivity across individuals show correspondingly less consistent clinical outcomes. Here we show that this seemingly idiosyncratic subcortical organization in fact reflects shared, fine-grained structure that can be recovered by modeling each individual's connectivity in a common functional space (connectivity hyperalignment, CHA), rather than relying on anatomical correspondence. Applying CHA to fMRI data collected during naturalistic movie viewing, we found that aligning subcortical voxels by their cortical connectivity, rather than their anatomical location, sharply increased cross-subject correspondence in both stimulus-evoked response and connectivity profiles. Critically, this alignment sharpened rather than blurred local structure: neighboring voxels became more functionally distinct from one another, and cortical connectivity targets became substantially more decodable across subjects. These results indicate that human subcortical nuclei possess a common fine-scale functional architecture that is masked by anatomical variability but recoverable at the individual level. This reframes a central methodological constraint in subcortical neuroimaging: rather than trading spatial resolution for signal quality via smoothing, group-level analyses can achieve voxel-level precision by aligning function rather than anatomy, opening a path to studying cortical-subcortical circuit organization in greater detail.

papers.title: Neurons in the lateral spinal nucleus give rise to the spinotectal component of the anterolateral system in the mouse
papers.abstract: The anterolateral system (ALS) originates from neurons in various regions of the spinal cord and conveys somatosensory information related to pain, skin temperature and itch to several brain targets. One component of the ALS is the spinotectal tract, which projects to the superior colliculus (SC) and is thought to underlie directed movements of the head towards a painful stimulus. Using anterograde and retrograde tracing, we demonstrate that the input from the spinal enlargements to the SC originates predominantly from neurons in the lateral spinal nucleus (LSN), many of which express calbindin. This input, which mainly targets the caudal and lateral parts of the SC, is somatotopically organised, and is associated with the clusters of Pitx2-expressing neurons that have been identified in previous studies. Since activation of Pitx2 neurons drives directed head movements, input from LSN neurons to the Pitx2 cells is likely to be a critical component of orientation and attention towards a noxious stimuli. We also provide evidence that spinotectal LSN cells receive excitatory synaptic input from neurons in superficial dorsal horn that express substance P or the gastrin-releasing peptide receptor (GRPR). Since GRPR neurons are strongly implicated in itch, our findings raise the possibility that the SC has a role in coordinating movements in response to pruritic stimuli.

papers.title: No Evidence of tACS-Primed Enhancement of Alpha Neurofeedback
papers.abstract: Neurofeedback shows promise as a clinical intervention, but its effectiveness is hindered by variability of response across individuals. One factor influencing neurofeedback success may be endogenous brain states, particularly the baseline power within target frequency bands. Transcranial alternating current stimulation (tACS) provides a potential mechanism to modulate these baseline frequency bands. This study explored whether tACS could effectively enhance participants' ability to gain neurofeedback control by increasing lateralised posterior alpha activity prior to engagement in a covert spatial attention-based neurofeedback task. Participants completed three counterbalanced sessions: 1) alpha tACS and active neurofeedback, 2) alpha tACS and sham neurofeedback, 3) gamma (40Hz) tACS and active neurofeedback. Neurofeedback performance was assessed via lateralised posterior alpha power shifts and Posner task reaction times. We identified no difference in reaction times or lateralised alpha power shifts across conditions. While participants reliably demonstrated lateralised posterior alpha patterns, consistent with the covert spatial attention neurofeedback protocol, no advantage of active neurofeedback over sham was observed. The lack of significant effects underscores the need for further rigorous tACS studies to identify the parameters essential for successful neural entrainment, and to evaluate its potential in enhancing neurofeedback efficacy.

papers.title: An information-borrowing Bayesian method for inferring high-dimensional population-level brain connectivity from small samples
papers.abstract: Estimating population-level dependence between brain regions is challenging when the number of regions greatly exceeds the number of individuals. We introduce an information-borrowing generalized Bayesian method for high-dimensional covariance estimation from region-level brain measurements. A divide-and-conquer parameterization separates marginal variances from correlation calibrations: an empirical \emph{pilot} correlation matrix--by default, obtained by standardizing a sample covariance matrix (SCM)--provides a reference structure that is adaptively calibrated through region-specific parameters shared across pairwise correlations, reducing the number of free parameters from $\mathcal{O}(d^2)$ to $\mathcal{O}(d)$ ($d$ is the number of regions) while guaranteeing a positive-definite covariance through the inclusion of a ridge term. Horseshoe priors on the calibration parameters enable selective borrowing and shrinkage of pilot information. Under suitable conditions on pilot accuracy, we establish theoretical guarantees for covariance estimation while retaining scalability in ultra-high-dimensional settings via a low-rank likelihood representation and a Woodbury-accelerated Hamiltonian Monte Carlo algorithm. Simulations showed lower estimation error than the SCM, bagging and iteratively refined principal orthogonal complement thresholding (POETRY). Applications to a semi-synthetic cortical-thickness and ADHD resting-state fMRI data revealed significant group differences in the default-mode--visual network and somatomotor network--limbic network blocks after Benjamini--Hochberg correction.

papers.title: Glycosaminoglycan presentation-dependent regulation of glial responses by Orion during Drosophila neuronal pruning
papers.abstract: Neuronal pruning refines neural circuits by eliminating unnecessary connections to ensure proper nervous system function. In Drosophila mushroom body gamma-neuron remodeling, the chemokine-like protein Orion is required for astrocyte infiltration and phagocytosis. This study investigated whether glial responses depend on how Orion is presented. We found that Orion interacts with glycosaminoglycans (GAG) associated to proteoglycans, which are essential for proper axon pruning. Tethering Orion to the gamma-neuron plasma membrane, mimicking glycosaminoglycan binding, was sufficient to induce astrocyte infiltration into axon bundles. However, membrane-bound Orion alone could not efficiently support phagocytosis, which additionally requires a soluble and mobile Orion pool. We also identified exosomes carrying GAG-bound Orion as potential mediators of neuronal remodeling. These findings provide the first evidence that glial infiltration can be uncoupled from phagocytosis, demonstrating that the mode of Orion presentation regulates distinct glial mechanisms during neuronal remodeling.

papers.title: Simultaneous multi-area recordings in macaque frontoparietal cortex during a manual object-interaction task
papers.abstract: Dexterous hand control is essential for daily activities and a top restoration priority for people with tetraplegia, yet neurophysiological datasets suitable for studying and decoding naturalistic hand behavior remain scarce. Most available recordings constrain movements to a small number of degrees of freedom or cover only a single stereotypical grasp-and-hold structure. Moreover, previous brain-computer interface (BCI) studies have largely relied on signals from a single cortical area, even though dexterous hand control is distributed across an interconnected frontoparietal network. To address these limitations, we designed a paradigm that elicits rich hand movements across 40 distinct hand-object interaction conditions. We recorded simultaneous frontoparietal activity with hand kinematics from a rhesus macaque performing them. Neural activity was recorded from the primary motor cortex, anterior intraparietal area, and ventral premotor cortex using microelectrode arrays spanning 1,920 channels, while a multi-camera markerless motion-capture system acquired video from which kinematics were extracted offline. The dataset comprises data from 20 sessions, including processed neural features, synchronized 3D coordinates of hand and elbow keypoints, and trial-level metadata including task conditions and event timing. We further provide technical validation, including a neural decoding benchmark with multiple algorithms for continuous keypoint coordination reconstruction. We found that cross-day and cross-task decoding performance varied among algorithms. Variation in channel availability leads to different performance degradation curves in different algorithms. This task-rich dataset offers a valuable resource for investigating the neural mechanisms of dexterous hand control and for advancing the performance of motor BCIs.

papers.title: Continuous Rod Noise and Nonlinear Synaptic Filtering Shape Signal Detection in the Primary Rod Pathway
papers.abstract: Rod photoreceptors are optimized to detect single photons, but their performance near absolute visual threshold is limited by intrinsic phototransduction noise. The two major components are discrete single-photon-like events and continuous fluctuations in outer-segment current. Although spontaneous rhodopsin activation is established as the source of discrete noise, the molecular origin of continuous noise remains controversial, and how these distinct noise sources influence signal processing at the first visual synapse is not fully understood. To address these questions, we combined genetic manipulation of rhodopsin, phosphodiesterase 6 (PDE6), and glutamic acid rich protein 2 (GARP2) with single-cell recordings from rods and rod-bipolar cells (RBCs) and pharmacological manipulation of mGluR6 signaling. Continuous noise was unaffected by reduced rhodopsin concentration but was strongly influenced by PDE6 expression and regulation, supporting basal PDE6 activity as a major source of continuous noise. Reducing either discrete or continuous noise increased signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) in rods, but these changes were differentially processed at the rod-to-RBC synapse. In WT retina, the nonlinear transformation increased SNR, whereas elevated continuous noise limited this increase. Conversely, reduced continuous noise increased rod SNR, which was maintained in RBCs and associated with a lower detection threshold. Pharmacological reduction of the mGluR6-dependent nonlinearity altered these genotype-dependent differences, indicating that nonlinear filtering is well matched to normal signal and noise distributions but does not fully compensate when presynaptic noise is experimentally altered. Together, our study identifies spontaneous PDE6 activity as a major source of continuous noise and demonstrates that continuous noise interacts with nonlinear processing at the first visual synapse to determine the fidelity and detection threshold of dim-light signals.

papers.title: Structural integrity moderates the cognitive bearing of dopamine clearance in aging
papers.abstract: Age-related cognitive decline in humans is well established, yet how neurobiological variations influence brain dynamics, and subsequently behavioral performance, remains insufficiently explored. Microscale accounts of cognitive aging revolve around attenuations in dopamine (DA) receptors and transporters (DAT). In contrast, macroscale accounts associate individual declines in cognitive performance with functional brain networks' reorganization and white-matter tracts' deterioration. We endeavor to bridge this gap with an amortized dopaminergic aging model (ADAM) which assembles aging brain twins by coupling dopaminergic modulation with structural connectomes to constrain emergent whole-brain dynamics. ADAM thereby augments established DAT decline with personalized estimates, through a reusable and generalizable estimator capable of disentangling neuromodulatory from structural contributions to age-related decline within each individual. To that end, we embed structural connectomes into a low-dimensional space exhibiting high reconstruction fidelity and -pseudonymized- individual identifiability. The spectrum of structural embeddings is subsequently updated with fMRI observations to estimate DA clearance timescales in 3,650 adults aged 36 to 95 years across five independent aging cohorts. Our analysis reveals an age-related elevation of DA clearance timescales. Critically, low performers exhibit elevated clearance in adults with marked structural degradation, and only within sliding age windows centred between 56 and 76 years. This supports a contribution of dopamine to aging, and reveals a structure- and age-conditional association between its clearance and cognitive performance. Our findings suggest that structural connectivity gates the macroscale reach of dopaminergic modulation, thus rendering the gain-control framework of neuromodulation mechanistically explicit across individuals and cohorts. ADAM therefore provides a biologically plausible framework that anchors interindividual variability in cognitive aging to perturbations in the dopaminergic system by learning cohort-scale mappings which can be shared across sites, establishing a transferable testbed for precision neuromodulation and future in-silico pharmacological trials.

papers.title: Imputation-Based Harmonization Mitigates Site Effects Without Data Leakage in Machine Learning Studies
papers.abstract: Neuroimaging studies that pool data across clinical sites often suffer from site effects --- variability in imaging measures that arises from technical heterogeneity across sites as opposed to true biological signal. While numerous harmonization methods have been proposed to remove site effects from imaging features, less attention has been placed on how to incorporate harmonization models into common machine-learning pipelines. We demonstrate that current approaches for integration either suffer from data leakage, fail to fully remove site effects from the target data, or attenuate true biological associations during the harmonization process. To address these issues, we propose Multiple Imputation for Removing Technical Heterogeneity (MIRTH), which uses imputed outcomes to harmonize the test data. We benchmark MIRTH's performance using both simulated and real-world volumetric data from the Alzheimer's Disease Neuroimaging Initiative and the Baltimore Longitudinal Study of Aging, demonstrating that MIRTH can achieve high predictive accuracy while avoiding inflated performance when the outcome is imbalanced across clinical sites.

papers.title: Distinct EEG microstate signatures across different pain types
papers.abstract: Pain is associated with dynamic brain reorganization. Electroencephalographic microstates can characterize transient large-scale brain states, yet findings across pain studies are inconsistent. Two features may contribute: conditions have been studied in isolation, and analytical pipelines vary widely. We applied a harmonized analysis pipeline across three pain conditions: capsaicininduced pain, assessed within participants against a pain-free baseline, and non-chronic and chronic back pain, each compared with matched controls. Using a five-minute resting-state electroencephalographic recordings we examined microstate topography, temporal expression and transition probabilities, and directly compared pain related differences across pain states. We identified five microstates (A-E), corresponding to auditory, visual, salience, and attentional networks. Capsaicin pain showed increased expression of microstate C and reduced expression of microstates A, D and E. Transitions were redistributed towards microstate C, indicating a shift toward salience-related processing at the expense of sensory and attentional dynamics. In clinical back pain, effects were smaller and diverged by pain type: non-chronic back pain showed lower microstate C occurrence, opposite in direction to the capsaicin effect, whereas chronic back pain showed lower microstate D global explained variance, suggesting salience and attentional differences in clinical pain. Direct comparisons showed weaker pain-related increases in microstate C expression in both clinical back pain groups than capsaicin pain, with additional differences involving microstates A, D and E. These findings argue against a unitary EEG microstate signature of pain and instead reveal pain-type-specific patterns of large-scale brain dynamics, with microstate C providing the clearest distinction between experimental and clinical pain.

papers.title: Perceptual sensitivity is explained by optimization for ecological tasks
papers.abstract: When asked to discriminate between two stimuli that differ along some dimension, such as intensity, frequency, or orientation, humans exhibit a smallest stimulus difference, or threshold, below which discrimination becomes impossible. These limits on perceptual sensitivity have traditionally been explained by internal noise. Contemporary theories instead link perceptual sensitivity to efficient coding of the natural environment but have not been comprehensively tested. Here, we measured the psychoacoustic sensitivity of a computational model optimized for everyday sound localization and recognition tasks. We used linear classifiers operating on the model's learned representations to estimate 1632 thresholds spanning the perceptual dimensions of sound. These model-derived thresholds closely matched thresholds measured behaviorally in humans on the same test battery. The results show that many classical psychophysical phenomena emerge from representations optimized for natural behavior and suggest that discrimination thresholds are determined by linear separability in these optimized representations, rather than intrinsic neural noise.

papers.title: Restoration of (nor)adrenergic-like Ca2+ signalling counteracts age-related motor decline

topics.name: Genetics, Aging, and Longevity in Model Organisms

papers.abstract: Aging disrupts neural function, but whether impaired noradrenergic control of brain metabolism contributes to functional decline remains unclear. Using genetically encoded fluorescent sensors we measured metabolic and signaling responses in neurons and glia of living Drosophila brains following stimulation with octopamine, the invertebrate analogue of noradrenaline. Aging was accompanied by neurodegeneration, reduced locomotion and enhanced oxidative whole-brain metabolism. Octopamine increased D-glucose uptake selectively in astrocytes and elevated L-lactate in both astrocytes and neurons, consistent with astrocytic glycolysis coupled to neuronal L-lactate uptake; monocarboxylate transporter inhibition caused selective astrocytic L-lactate accumulation. In aged animals octopamine-evoked metabolic responses in astrocytes and neural Ca2+ transients were markedly reduced. This impairment was associated with lower expression of adrenoceptor-like tyramine 1 receptor (Tyr1R). Selective Tyr1R overexpression in (nor)adrenergic-like Tdc2 neurons prolonged lifespan, restored Ca2+ signalling and improved locomotor performance. These findings identify Tyr1R-dependent Ca2+ signalling as an age-sensitive regulator of brain metabolism and motor function.

papers.title: Translating functional brain activity between humans and monkeys
papers.abstract: Comparing brain responses across species is essential for identifying models of human cognition and testing theories of brain evolution, but differences in brain size, measurement techniques, and signal dynamics make it challenging. Here we collected dense fMRI data in macaques and humans using the same movies, static-image sequences, and tasks, and developed a multivariate analysis method that aligns neural representations temporally and spatially. The resulting data-driven framework provides a quantitative translation of brain responses among individuals and between species. Using this framework, we uncovered a broadly conserved cross-species hierarchy of retinotopic visual areas and whole-brain correspondence. Yet within this structure, we found that higher-order macaque areas shared more information with lower-order human areas, particularly during movies, providing evidence of species differences. We also identified potential macaque precursors to human regions involved in high-level cognition, including theory-of-mind and reading. These results offer a blueprint for common representational principles across species.

papers.title: Distinct population dimensions separate sensory adaptation and expectation-related signals in visual cortex
papers.abstract: Mismatch negativity is conventionally quantified as a scalar response-amplitude difference between rare deviant and repeated standard stimuli, leaving its organization at the neuronal population level unresolved. We recorded population activity in mouse primary visual cortex (V1) during visual oddball and control paradigms while testing contributions from anterior cingulate cortex (ACC) input using optogenetic inhibition. Mismatch modulated firing rates bidirectionally and these changes largely canceled out on average, yet produced robustly separable population activity patterns. On the stimulus-encoding manifold, repeated standard exposure produced standard-specific response attenuation and a shared rotation of standard and deviant representations, revealing a component not isolated by conventional stimulus-specific adaptation and deviance-detection contrasts. Off the manifold, standards and deviants occupied opposing positions along an ACC-modulated axis consistent with expectation confirmation and violation. Thus, visual mismatch responses engage separable transformations of stimulus representations and expectation-related population activity, with ACC input selectively contributing to the latter while not significantly affecting stimulus encoding or on-manifold adaptation.

papers.title: Hyperexcitable but seizure-free: hippocampal network dysfunction in a Wolfram syndrome model
papers.abstract: Wolfram syndrome (WS) is a rare, life-limiting progressive neurodegenerative disorder caused by pathogenic variants in the WFS1 gene. It is a prototype endoplasmic reticulum (ER) stress disorder, and the mechanisms underlying neurological phenotypes in WS remain incompletely understood. Although WFS1 protein is abundant in the hippocampus, the role of this region in WS remains relatively understudied. Here we characterize hippocampal function across scales in mice carrying a patient orthologous Wfs1 variant (p.W542*) on both alleles. Male mutants lose excitatory synapses, and dissociated hippocampal neurons are markedly hyperexcitable yet generate no increase in network bursting and no shift in network criticality, indicating that their additional firing is not recruited into coordinated population activity. This finding translates in vivo wherein intracranial electroencephalogram (EEG) recordings show no epileptiform activity or seizures in either sex, with no hippocampal astrogliosis, alongside a male-specific reduction in hippocampal low-gamma power. Additionally, EEG demonstrates a sex-specific disruption of sleep, which parallels a sex-divergent synaptic phenotype. Mutant male mice show impaired hippocampus-dependent fear memory and reduced voluntary motor activity. Taken together, we propose that cellular hyperexcitability in the WS hippocampus does not translate into increased network bursting, potentially due to disproportionate loss of excitatory synapses. This dissociation may provide a functional substrate for the neurological features of WS.

papers.title: Remembering touch: Somatosensory cortex supports long-term memory for dynamic vibrotactile patterns.
papers.abstract: The neural substrates of tactile long-term memory (LTM) in humans remain poorly understood, as relatively few neuroimaging studies have addressed this question. Here, we asked whether retrieval of tactile stimulation engages modality-specific representations in the primary and secondary somatosensory cortices (S1 and S2), alongside domain-general retrieval networks. Participants learned 16 tactile trajectories, each presented for 1.2 s on the left thumb through sequential activation of 10 vibrating dots on a Braille-like display. Three learning sessions within one week were followed by a recognition test during functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI). In the final sample (n = 26), we contrasted BOLD responses during successful recognition of learned stimuli with those during correct rejection of novel stimuli. Successful recognition was associated with increased activity in contralateral S1 and S2, alongside activation in the hippocampus as well as frontal and parietal regions implicated in memory retrieval. A psychophysiological interaction analysis (PPI) further revealed increased task-dependent connectivity between the hippocampus and contralateral S1 and S2 during successful recognition. Together, these findings suggest that tactile long-term memory retrieval relies on coordinated hippocampal-somatosensory interactions and may engage long-term memory representations in somatosensory cortex.

papers.title: Inhibitory budget matching constrains homeostatic plasticity in competitive spiking networks
papers.abstract: Competitive spiking networks can form sensory representations through local synaptic plasticity and lateral inhibition. A canonical example is the Diehl-Cook architecture, in which Poisson-encoded sensory inputs drive excitatory neurons through spike-timing-dependent plasticity (STDP), while a separate inhibitory population imposes competition between excitatory units. In most implementations this competitive circuit is fixed, although inhibitory synapses are plastic in cortical circuits and contribute to excitation-inhibition balance. It therefore remains unclear under which conditions biologically motivated inhibitory plasticity can replace fixed lateral competition without disrupting representation learning. Here we study this question in a competitive STDP network trained on MNIST. We compare fixed inhibition with a Vogels-style inhibitory STDP rule, slow homeostatic inhibition, and a budget-constrained slow homeostatic rule that conserves the total inhibitory input received by each excitatory neuron. A fixed-inhibition operating-point map showed that stability depends on the dynamical regime: 56% of tested fixed-inhibition runs completed training, whereas stronger inhibition at higher input gain produced runaway activity. The reference regime g = 2.0, wIE = 10.0, selected for subsequent comparisons, combined complete stability across replicate initializations with high classification performance (84.3 {+/-} 0.6% after 30,000 training examples). In this regime, the budget-constrained rule was stable in all replicate runs when its inhibitory budget matched the fixed-inhibition reference (BI = 3990), reaching 83.5 {+/-} 0.6% accuracy with firing-rate and inhibitory-conductance statistics close to fixed inhibition, whereas a mismatched budget (BI = 7980) produced runaway activity in every replicate. Parameter maps showed that Vogels-derived iSTDP was broadly but not uniformly stable (90% runs completed), while slow homeostatic inhibition was even more broadly stable (96%). Budget-constrained stability depended strongly on the conserved budget, i.e., low and matched budgets were stable or nearly stable, intermediate budgets were mixed, and BI = 7980 failed in all tested runs. These results show that inhibitory plasticity in competitive STDP networks is not governed by a local homeostatic update alone. Stable plastic competition depends jointly on the operating regime and on an inhibitory budget that fixes the total strength of competition while allowing local inhibitory weights to adapt. Mechanistically, budget matching separates local redistribution of inhibitory weights from changes in total inhibitory drive, preventing plasticity from shifting the network away from a stable competitive state. This identifies inhibitory budget matching as a practical design principle for replacing fixed inhibition with plastic, homeostatically regulated competition in STDP-based spiking networks.

papers.title: Machine-assisted systematic review and meta-analysis of citrus flavonoids in streptozotocin-induced painful diabetic neuropathy
papers.abstract:
BackgroundNeuropathic pain is a common and debilitating condition with persistently poor translation from preclinical research to effective clinical therapies. Preclinical systematic reviews and meta-analyses (SRMAs) can provide more robust estimates of intervention effects and help identify sources of bias and heterogeneity, but their use is limited by the time and effort required to synthesise rapidly expanding literatures.

Automation may help overcome these barriers.

MethodsWe developed Neuropathic Pain - Systematic Online Living Evidence Summaries (NP-SOLES), a machine-assisted approach used in this study to support systematic identification of animal studies relevant to neuropathic pain. Using NP-SOLES, we conducted a pilot systematic review and meta-analysis of controlled animal studies assessing the effects of citrus flavonoids on thermal and mechanical pain-related outcomes in streptozotocin-induced models of painful diabetic neuropathy.

ResultsIn this pilot application, machine-assisted evidence synthesis supported reduced manual screening burden, illustrating the potential of such approaches to facilitate timely preclinical SRMAs. Fourteen studies met inclusion criteria for meta-analysis on thermal pain-related outcomes. Pooled estimates suggested a reduction in thermal pain-related behaviours following flavonoid treatment; however, substantial heterogeneity and widespread methodological limitations were observed. Nine studies were eligible for qualitative analysis on mechanical pain-related outcomes, which showed an overall reduction in pain-related behaviours following treatment but had similar methodological limitations. Reporting of key measures to reduce risk of bias, including randomisation and blinding, were consistently poor, and subgroup analyses were constrained by sparse data.

ConclusionsAvailable evidence from preclinical animal studies suggests a potential analgesic effect of citrus flavonoids on thermal and mechanical pain-related outcomes in diabetic neuropathy models, but confidence in this estimate is limited by significant risks of bias. More rigorously designed and transparently reported preclinical studies are required before clinical translation can be justified.

papers.title: Cryo-EM structures of insect IRs reveal the structural adaptations of a glutamate receptor ancestor for environmental sensing
papers.abstract: Ionotropic receptors (IRs) are an ancient, massively expanded family of sensory ion channels that mediate chemical, thermal, and hygrosensory detection across invertebrates. Derived from synaptic ionotropic glutamate receptors (iGluRs), IRs achieve this diverse tuning by assembling conserved co-receptor subunits with highly divergent tuning subunits into obligate heteromers. To understand how this architecture arose from a glutamate receptor ancestor we report cryo-EM structures of three insect IR complexes spanning the major functional subfamilies: IR8a/IR75b, IR25a/IR76b, and IR25a/IR93a/IR40a. All IR complexes retain the tiered iGluR architecture but adopt a distinctive splayed, non-swapped architecture that our phylogenetic reconstructions relate to a sister branch of glutamate delta (GluD) receptors. Our structures reveal a novel, co-receptor-specific helical beam feature that dictates stoichiometry by interlocking the co-receptors and separating the tuning subunits, at the cost of abolishing ligand binding in co-receptors. Comparison of IR8a- and IR25a- containing complexes further illuminates the structural basis of subfamily specificity yielding a predictive code of co-receptor assembly. Lastly, we identify IR-specific coupling mechanisms between the gating machineries of tuning and co-receptor subunits, offering a model for the cooperative gating of IRs. These analyses illuminate how an ancient synaptic receptor was architecturally remodeled into a multimodal family of sensory receptors that drive critical behaviors across invertebrates.
